research.abstract: Abstract The deep-learning language model offers promising approaches to molecular design. However, existing models typically exhibit one or more of the following limitations: structural constraints, confinement to a single task, and lack of cross-domain capability (e.g., protein-to-ligand generation). Inspired by GPT’s success in language modeling, we introduce ProLigGPT, a seq2seq autoregressive model based on GPT-2 and trained on ∼1.9 million protein-ligand pairs without 3D structures. ProLigGPT supports tasks including de novo ligand generation and scaffold-based molecular design for target proteins. Benchmarking against three state-of-the-art structure-based models across eight representative target proteins, ProLigGPT demonstrated superior performance on comprehensive metrics. Through systematic evaluations of ProLigGPT’s interpretability, we find that ProLigGPT uses the full protein sequence to generate target-aware ligands, unlike pocket-based strategies that depend only on residues near the binding site. Applying ProLigGPT to Pl3Kα inhibitor design successfully yielded inhibitors with a novel scaffold and inhibitors derived from a known scaffold, demonstrating that ProLigGPT can reach beyond the boundaries of known chemical space. Finally, we validated the generalization ability of ProLigGPT on Target T1, which lacks a crystal structure and known inhibitors, confirming that ProLigGPT can design inhibitors solely from sequence information. These findings highlight the promise of language models in designing ligands for target proteins free from structural constraints, offering a flexible and scalable framework for exploring vast chemical spaces in drug discovery.

items.title: Genomic signatures of positive selection and relaxed selective constraints associated with convergent dietary specialisation
items.summary: Island radiations provide ideal frameworks for studying the molecular basis of convergent evolution. research.abstract: ABSTRACT Island radiations provide ideal frameworks for studying the molecular basis of convergent evolution. The rapid diversification of Dysdera spiders in Canary Islands provides a striking example, with repeated dietary shifts towards specialisation on woodlice, accompanied by morphological, metabolic, and behavioural modifications that facilitate the exploitation of this heavy-metal-rich prey. Here, we investigate two independent events of dietary specialisation on different islands. By analysing six high-quality genome-assemblies, including three newly generated in this study, we investigate the genomic signals of positive selection and relaxed selection in protein-coding genes, upstream regulatory regions, and gene family turnover rates. We detected signatures of positive selection associated with the two specialists, accompanied by a twofold increase in gene loss rates relative to generalist ancestors. Notably, positive selection targeted a smaller, functionally coherent set of genes, potentially involved in detoxification likely through heavy metal excretion. In contrast, relaxation of selection affected a broader set of genes associated with functions that may have become dispensable under the new dietary regime. Furthermore, we found contractions in gene families associated with vesicular transport, potentially reflecting a reduced reliance on vesicle-mediated metal accumulation. Overall, our findings suggest that similar ecological pressures can drive parallel, yet non-identical, adaptive and non-adaptive responses, pointing to partially predictable evolutionary trajectories in an island radiation.

items.title: Phylogeography and transmission dynamics of the 2025-2026 Utah-Arizona measles outbreak: a retrospective genomic epidemiology study

However, epidemiological data alone are not sufficient to infer transmission patterns. MethodsAs part of the local and state-wide outbreak…

research.abstract: Abstract Background Measles outbreaks are increasing in frequency globally as vaccine coverage decreases. During the 2025-26 Utah-Arizona border outbreak, identifying where and between whom transmission occurred was essential for directing control measures. However, epidemiological data alone are not sufficient to infer transmission patterns. Methods As part of the local and state-wide outbreak investigation, we conducted amplicon-based whole genome sequencing on residual diagnostic samples from confirmed measles cases collected from June 15, 2025–April 30, 2026. We reconstructed viral dispersal across Utah using Bayesian phylogeographic analyses. We evaluated genetic distance thresholds for identifying recent transmission by comparing single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based genetic clusters with known epidemiologic linkages. We then assessed pairwise exposures associated with genetically supported transmission linkage using logistic regression, accounting for network and spatial dependence between pairs. Findings We generated 509 high-quality whole measles virus genomes from 913 patients. In 2025, most viral dispersal events (67.9%) originated in Southwest Utah and Mohave County, Arizona, where the first cases were reported. By 2026, most viral spread (60.5%) occurred outside of this area. A threshold of 0 SNPs identified epidemiologically linked pairs of individuals with a sensitivity of 77.4% and specificity of 92.3%. Household membership (odds ratio (OR): 219.10, 95% credible interval (CI): 112.66-325.53), participation in the same sport (OR: 15.19, 95% CI: 9.75-20.63), and attendance at the same school (OR: 51.5, 95% CI: 36.38-66.61) were independently associated with transmission linkage. Increasing distance between households was associated with reduced odds of linkage (OR: 0.46: 95% CI 0.44-0.48). Interpretation Repeated introductions of measles virus from southwestern Utah seeded transmission elsewhere in Utah, with household, school, and sports exposures contributing to onward transmission. Validated genome-based linkage measures can complement contact tracing by helping public health teams identify likely transmission networks and prioritize investigation when resources are constrained. Funding Epidemiology and Laboratory Capacity (ELC) program at the CDC Research in Context Evidence before this study We searched PubMed and medRxiv as of October 6, 2026 for studies about measles genomic or molecular epidemiology, measles virus transmission modelling, and application of whole genome sequencing of measles virus. English language search terms included “measles”, “measles virus”, “phylodynamic”, “genomic epidemiology”, “molecular epidemiology”, “transmission modelling”, “transmission dynamics”, “sequencing”, “whole genome sequencing”, and “WGS”. Previous studies have primarily utilized N450 sequencing in their outbreak assessments, including phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses. More recent studies have utilized whole genome sequencing to perform phylogenetic analysis and have overlaid some epidemiological data to assess transmission. To our knowledge, no studies have combined epidemiological and whole genome sequencing data to quantitatively assess drivers of transmission. Added value of this study We integrate detailed epidemiological data with whole genome sequencing, providing a comprehensive analysis of geographic spread and key drivers of transmission in the Utah-Arizona border outbreak. We generated whole genome sequences for 56% of confirmed cases, high sequence coverage that enabled us to identify an appropriate genomic threshold and approximate direct transmission links. Our findings illustrate a change in geographic transmission as the outbreak persisted and highlighted household, school, and sports based transmission as primary sources of exposure. Implications of all the available evidence Our findings demonstrate the utility of measles surveillance using whole genome sequencing paired with epidemiological data. As measles outbreaks increase in frequency, new approaches are needed to characterize the key drivers of transmission. By integrating epidemiologic and genomic data, we identified genomic thresholds for transmission that can be applied in settings where extensive epidemiologic data are unavailable. Ultimately, utilizing genomic and epidemiological data together will strengthen our surveillance of future measles outbreaks.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Although direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and Methods We conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee ≥60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded ≥30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. Results In the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. Conclusion An explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

items.title: On estimating the effective sample size of phylogenetic trees in an autocorrelated chain
items.summary: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC…

research.abstract: Estimating the effective sample size (ESS) is fundamental in Bayesian phylogenetic inference to account for autocorrelation in MCMC samples. While methods for continuous parameters are well established, the discrete and high-dimensional nature of treespace poses substantial challenges. In this paper, we introduce a new approach based on Conditional Clade Distributions (CCDs) to emulate MCMC chains with known ESS bounds. We compare existing tree ESS estimators with novel approaches that utilize CCDs as tractable tree distributions, as well as a new probabilistic estimator based on differences in clade frequencies between independent chains. Using our emulated chains from both simulated and real datasets, we assess estimators for their ability to recover the true ESS (accuracy), their insensitivity to the removal of autocorrelated samples from the chain (stability), and their tolerance to combining multiple chains together (robustness). We further examine how multimodality and poor inter-mode chain mixing can compromise the reliability of tree ESS estimates. These findings indicate that our new CCD-based estimators perform comparably to existing approaches with respect to accuracy, stability, and robustness. In contrast, the probabilistic estimator and two previously recommended methods incur prohibitive computational costs for long chains. Together, these results establish a new framework for evaluating tree ESS estimators using CCD-based emulated MCMC chains and demonstrate their performance and current limitations in practical phylogenetic analyses. The expanded suite of tree ESS estimators is available in the user-friendly TreeStat2 software package for BEAST 2.

research.abstract: PREPRINT-25 (v1.0.0 Empirical Preprint) • 100% Native Rust bio-suite-supervisor Across 544 Verified NCBI Records (L = 52,227 Aligned Columns) We reconstruct the Paleozoic-to-Anthropocene phylogenomic radiation, kleptocnidae/chemosensory/terpenoid enzyme evolution, and multi-compartment marine demographic history of the global radiation of Nudibranchia and allied Nudipleura (spanning Suborder Cladobranchia [Berghia stephanieae, Spurilla braziliana, Hermissenda emurai, Facelina bostoniensis, Phestilla fuscostriata, Tritonia tetraquetra, Melibe leonina, Dendronotus frondosus, Doto coronata, Dermatobranchus otome] and Suborder Doridina [Hexabranchus sanguineus, Polycera hedgpethi, Nembrotha kubaryana, Doris pseudoargus, Peltodoris atromaculata, Dendrodoris krusensternii, Phyllidia elegans, Phyllidiella pustulosa, Cadlina japonica, Chromodoris annae, C. lochi, Goniobranchus leopardus, Doriprismatica atromarginata, Glossodoris acosti, Hypselodoris whitei], rooted on Pleurobranchida and Tectipleura outgroups Aplysia californica and Elysia chlorotica) across 544 active verified NCBI sequence records (plus 6 autonomously quarantined GenBank UNVERIFIED anomalies) comprising a 64-taxon, 18-locus supermatrix (L = 52,227 aligned columns), 48 nuclear functional coding sequences, and 12 regional and multi-locus cohorts (12 x N = 36 = 432 isolates). Executed end-to-end via autonomous Native Rust bio-suite-supervisor optimization across 32 candidate RuNIE chains (total runtime 236.53 s; B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC generations with 20% burn-in), RY3 purine/pyrimidine recoding under GTR+F+R4 reduces heterobranch compositional heterogeneity by 85.8% (RCFV = 0.0052 vs. 0.0365, ln L = -600,241.59), dating Root Heterobranchia to 284.6 Ma, Crown Nudipleura to 236.4 Ma, Crown Nudibranchia (Cladobranchia vs. Doridina) to 198.2 Ma, and Crown Chromodoridoidea to 52.8 Ma. Native Rust quartet multispecies coalescent inference (runie-quartet-coalescent across 18 gene trees and 11,436,768 quartets in 43.90 ms) recovers 8,586,986 satisfied quartets (normalized Q = 0.7508, mean LPP = 0.8864) while ABBA-BABA tests quantify reticulate allele sharing across Indo-Pacific Chromodoris/Goniobranchus mimicry rings and Phyllidiidae spongivores. Sixty-one-state Goldman-Yang codon models identify strong purifying constraint on cnidosac C-type lectin/cathepsin cores (omega_0 = 0.000) and Hsp70/BiP/DnaJ heatwave chaperones alongside 4D Bayes Empirical Bayes diversifying selection on rhinophore nAChR/mGluR/Kv receptors (peak BEB omega = 7.12) and CYP3A29/CYP4F1 terpenoid-sequestering monooxygenase pockets (foreground omega_fg = 0.001, peak BEB omega = 2.75). Finally, 12 coupled Bayesian coalescent skylines contrast Last Glacial Maximum shelf-exposure bottlenecks, Holocene Coral Triangle lagoon expansions, and pelagic Glaucus gyre stability against sharp locus-specific Ne compressions at nuclear Histone H3 / terpenoid-linked loci relative to neutral mitochondrial COX1 (1Ne) and Katoh E-INS-i-aligned ribosomal 16S/28S rDNA (4Ne) reservoirs. Autonomous 100% Native Rust bio-suite-supervisor synthesis across 544 verified NCBI records (L = 52,227 aligned columns, 32 RuNIE chains, 11.44M quartets, 300k MCMC generations in 236.53 s) resolves the 284.6 Ma-to-present global radiation, kleptocnidae & CYP3A29 terpenoid evolution, and 12 regional vs. multi-locus skylines of Nudibranchia. research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 16 loci (L = 37,741 aligned columns; Carabidae, Scarabaeidae, Coccinellidae, Cerambycidae, Chrysomelidae, and Curculionidae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three independent PopSets (Dendroctonus ponderosae, Harmonia axyridis, and Pterostichus melanarius) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The hyperdiverse radiation of beetles (Order Coleoptera) across terrestrial ecosystems was propelled by key physiological and enzymatic innovations—from cursorial predation and pygidial chemical defense in Adephaga (Carabidae) and hindgut microbial fermentation in Scarabaeiformia (Scarabaeidae) to cryptonephridic Malpighian tubule water conservation in Cucujiformia (Coccinellidae) and horizontally transferred plant cell wall degrading enzymes (GH5, GH28, and GH45) in Phytophaga (Cerambycidae, Chrysomelidae, and Curculionidae). Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across a 16-locus, 64-species supermatrix (L = 37,741 aligned columns with 15,440 parsimony-informative sites) coupled with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three localized population datasets benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE with *LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST. Our dated chronogram and codon selection models anchor Crown Coleoptera at 295.0 Ma, Cucujiformia cryptonephridic water conservation at 224.8 Ma, and the Phytophaga cell-wall enzyme radiation at 174.0 Ma, revealing strong purifying constraint on GH28 pectinases (omega = 0.2251) alongside diversifying selection on CYP6 detoxification monooxygenases (omega = 1.0657). Across the three localized PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve an 11.1-fold Anthropocene drought and winter-warming outbreak expansion in the mountain pine beetle Dendroctonus ponderosae (Ne = 184,439 to 2,052,657), an 88.1% biocontrol founder bottleneck followed by a 37.4-fold invasive bridgehead explosion in Harmonia axyridis (Ne = 62,937 to 2,351,789), and an 83.0% agrochemical intensification crash followed by beetle-bank corridor recovery in the epigean predator Pterostichus melanarius, while demonstrating that *MAFFT progressive alignment consumes 80.1% of external pipeline runtime compared to a 21.0-fold end-to-end speedup in Native Rust. items.title: Clinical and neurohormonal correlates of plasma TNF-α in a Zambian outpatient cohort.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic inflammation persists in populations with high HIV and tuberculosis (TB) burden, even during suppressive therapy. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) is a key mediator, but its correlates beyond infectious status remain unclear in people living with HIV on stable antiretroviral therapy and who are virologically suppressed. We investigated clinical, metabolic, and neurohormonal correlates of TNF-α in a Zambian cohort. Methods This was a cross-sectional study, which included 227 adults recruited from the outpatient medical clinic at Livingstone University Teaching Hospital in the Southern Province of Zambia. Simple and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed to determine independent associations with plasma TNF-α levels. Models were adjusted for HIV serostatus and history of TB. Standardized beta coefficients (β_std) were computed to compare the relative magnitude of associations across predictors measured on different scales. Results Among 227 participants, 64.8% were living with HIV (95.3% on integrase strand transfer inhibitor-based ART) and 14.0% had a history of tuberculosis. In multivariable analysis, the strongest independent associations with TNF-α were observed within the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS): angiotensin II (β = 1.18 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.51) and aldosterone (β = 0.884 per pg/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.47). Living with HIV serostatus was also independently associated with higher TNF-α (β = 2581.1 pg/mL, p = 0.018; β_std = 0.19), while the history of TB was not. Significant metabolic factors associated with TNF-α levels included VLDL (β = 4397.4 per mmol/L, p = 0.038; β_std = 0.16) and triglycerides (β = 1971.6 per mmol/L, p = 0.034; β_std = 0.17). Inflammatory markers sST2 (β = 104.4 per ng/mL, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.31), IL-17 A (β = 1.137 per pg/mL, p = 0.003; β_std = 0.21), and D-dimer (β = 0.037 per pg/mL, p = 0.001; β_std = 0.22) were independently associated, as was plasma potassium (β = 107.3 per mmol/L, p < 0.001; β_std = 0.46). Renin, IL-6, IL-5, hs-CRP, and left ventricular mass were not associated with TNF-α. Conclusion In this high-burden population, RAAS activation was an independent correlate of TNF-α, exceeding the effect of HIV serostatus. These findings support the hypothesis that RAAS inhibition may have anti-inflammatory effects; however, this remains to be tested in prospective and interventional studies.

items.title: From junk to deleterious: Natural subtelomeric repeat amplifications impact fitness and cellular phenotypes in yeast
items.summary: Eukaryotic genomes exhibit astounding levels of complexity. Much of this complexity resides in repetitive DNA thought to evolve neutrally, meaning that its impact on fitness is so small that natural selection cannot act efficiently to favor or purge it. Yet, repetitive DNA greatly facilitates the generation of structural variants (SVs), which fuel evolution with both adaptive and deleterious…

research.abstract: Abstract Eukaryotic genomes exhibit astounding levels of complexity. Much of this complexity resides in repetitive DNA thought to evolve neutrally, meaning that its impact on fitness is so small that natural selection cannot act efficiently to favor or purge it. Yet, repetitive DNA greatly facilitates the generation of structural variants (SVs), which fuel evolution with both adaptive and deleterious genetic variation. How SVs involving initially neutral repetitive DNA can bring new evolutionarily meaningful impacts is not well understood, in part because finding and interpreting molecular signatures of these transitions using comparative genomics over long evolutionary timescales is challenging. Here, we document one such transition over a microevolutionary timescale using budding yeast population genomics. We characterize multiple massive amplifications of the Y’ element, a highly polymorphic and dispensable subtelomeric tandem repeat. We uncover extreme structural diversity in Y’ tandem amplifications among near-isogenic strains and show that these amplifications bring a significant fitness cost. We further link Y’ amplifications with transcriptome rewiring, heightened DNA replication stress sensitivity, and DNA damage response activation. Together, our results support a model by which massive subtelomeric tandem amplification pushed a repetitive DNA family outside of effective neutrality to become deleterious. Significance Statement Extant eukaryotic genomes harbor vast amounts of repetitive DNA elements hypothesized to be non-functional and to have accumulated and persisted through neutral evolutionary processes without substantially affecting organismal fitness. Here, we report that an entire non-functional DNA family evolved out of effective neutrality in the baker’s yeast S. cerevisiae . The Y′ elements, a family of non-functional subtelomeric repeats, have repeatedly undergone dramatic tandem amplifications at chromosome ends across independently evolving S. cerevisiae populations. We show that these amplifications confer fitness defects of sufficient magnitude to be considered non-neutral within the population-genetic environment of the species. These amplifications are associated with numerous cellular phenotypes that likely contribute to this fitness cost, including core transcriptome rewiring, heightened sensitivity to DNA replication stress and increased DNA damage.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bedaquiline (BDQ), pretomanid (Pa) and linezolid (LZD)-based (BPaL) regimens have transformed rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB) treatment. However, resistance to these drugs is increasingly reported, while longitudinal data integrating clinical, phenotypic and genomic evolution remain limited. CASE PRESENTATION: We report a fatal case of recurrent RR-TB in a 40-year-old South African woman with HIV infection who received BPaL therapy. Following treatment completion, recurrent disease was complicated by pregnancy, treatment interruption and loss to follow-up. She subsequently re-presented with advanced cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis and respiratory failure. Despite re-initiation of BPaL, she deteriorated and died from septic shock. Routine drug susceptibility testing, available posthumously, confirmed resistance to BDQ, Pa and LZD. Seven sequential Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates collected during treatment underwent minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) testing and whole-genome sequencing. All demonstrated phenotypic resistance to the three BPaL drugs. Serial genomic analysis identified progressive Rv0678 diversification associated with a two-fold increase in BDQ MIC, while resistance-associated rrl and fbiC mutations remained comparatively stable despite persistently elevated LZD and Pa MICs. CONCLUSIONS: This case demonstrates the interaction of treatment interruption, delayed resistance detection and continued within-host bacterial adaptation during BPaL therapy. Longitudinal phenotypic and genomic findings revealed distinct resistance trajectories among BPaL drugs, highlighting the importance of treatment retention, timely susceptibility testing and genomic surveillance for preserving BPaL effectiveness.

research.abstract: Abstract Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue represents a vast clinical resource, yet three-dimensional imaging and omics-wide molecular profiling remain largely incompatible because current antigen retrieval and clearing can degrade nucleic acids. We developed REZCUE, a depth-invariant antigen retrieval chemistry that enables 3D multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging of intact FFPE tissue while quantitatively preserving DNA, RNA, and protein for multi-omics analyses. REZCUE restores antigenicity in tissue archived for up to 30 years, supports 160 commercial whole-IgG antibodies across tissue types, and enables imaging to 6 mm depth. Imaging before destructive molecular profiling establishes a 3D spatial reference for registering molecular assays to intact tissue architecture. REZCUE enabled multi-modal mapping of spatial niches of the mouse brain and identified a human breast tumor compartment not distinguishable by conventional section-based spatial-omics, revealed after integrating 3D image-guided segmentation with spatial transcriptomics, mass spectrometry, miRNA sequencing, and whole-genome sequencing. In short, REZCUE transforms archived FFPE specimens into spatially registered, molecularly resolved, 3D substrates for sequential spatial multi-omic interrogation. Graphical abstract

research.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) remains the most economically devastating pathogen of the global swine industry, with frequent genetic recombination and continuous lineage replacement driving its rapid evolution. Hubei Province, a major swine-producing hub in central China, endures substantial PRRSV disease pressure, yet the current epidemiological and evolutionary landscape of circulating strains remains poorly characterized. In this study, 1478 clinical samples were collected from 12 prefecture-level cities between 2024 and 2025 and subjected to RT-PCR detection, ORF5 sequencing, virus isolation, and complete genome analysis. The detection rate among clinical samples was 26.32%, highest in nursery pigs (32.65%). Phylogenetic analysis of 136 ORF5 sequences revealed lineage 1 dominance (66.18%), comprising NADC30-like (38.24%) and NADC34-like (27.94%) strains, followed by lineage 8 (24.26%), lineage 5 (5.15%), and lineage 3 (4.41%). Six isolates were recovered, and whole-genome analysis identified lineage-specific NSP2 deletion patterns and a recombinant strain (LW HP) bearing a JXA1-like backbone with NADC30-like insertions. Selection pressure analysis ranked Nsp2 as the least-constrained gene (dN/dS = 0.3065; purifying selection), with positively selected codons in GP5 and the NSP2 hypervariable region. These findings delineate the current epidemic status and genetic characteristics of PRRSV in central China, providing critical data for regional prevention and vaccine development.

research.abstract: DEG (Degradation of periplasmic proteins) proteases are ATP-independent serine endopeptidases found in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes including plants. They are considered to be key regulators of development and stress tolerance in plants. In this study, a comprehensive genome-wide analysis identified 19 serine protease-like DEG family proteins in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.), revealing their structural diversity, domain architecture, and regulatory potential. Physiochemical profiling showed a predominance of acidic isoelectric points (pI), variable protein lengths (169–1083 amino acids), and differential stability indices. Subcellular localization predicted most DEG proteases to reside in the chloroplast, with others distributed across cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and peroxisome. Domain analysis confirmed the universal presence of the trypsin domain, with varying numbers of PDZ domains and additional conserved motifs among paralogs. Evolutionary divergence analysis of StDEG genes and their orthologs from six Solanaceae species as well as Arabidopsis thaliana, Oryza sativa, and Zea mays revealed dN/dS ratios below one for all orthologous pairs, suggesting that StDEG genes have evolved under strong purifying selection and remained highly conserved throughout plant evolution. Gene ontology annotations linked DEG proteases to key biological functions including PSII repair, photoinhibition, and chloroplast organization, alongside protein catabolism and light stimulus response. Promoter analysis revealed an abundance of cis-regulatory elements (CREs), particularly light-responsive motifs, along with hormone and stress-related elements such as ABRE, ARE, and MBS. Expression profiling across eight developmental tissues demonstrated tissue-specific expression patterns, with strong transcript accumulation of selected DEG members in senescent leaf, stolon, shoot apex, and tuber. Interestingly, several splice variants showed unique expression dynamics, including stage-specific and stress-induced activation. Upon exposure to abiotic and hormonal cues, 16 DEG proteases displayed significant transcriptional modulation, particularly under light, ABA, and Zeatin treatments, with notable fold changes reaching up to 26-fold in certain variants. These findings highlight the functional versatility of DEG proteases in potato development and stress adaptation, especially their responsiveness to light and hormonal stimuli. The characterization of these proteases paves the way for future studies on their roles in crop resilience and genome editing applications.

research.abstract: Abstract Steady-state molecular profiles incompletely capture the regulatory programs through which genetic variation influences complex disease, particularly programs that emerge only when cells are perturbed. Here, we introduce Perturbscape, a computational framework that learns multiscale gene programs for individual perturbations in a CRISPR Perturb-seq screen using linear and nonlinear contrastive approaches alongside complementary program-learning methods, and integrates them with human genetics to prioritize disease-relevant genes, perturbations and downstream regulatory pathways. Across 15,859 perturbation-by-context profiles from 7 Perturb-seq systems and 53 complex diseases and traits (mean GWAS N=291K), perturbation-induced programs showed up to 4.3-fold higher heritability informativeness than analogous steady-state multi-tissue gene prioritization, and retained significant conditional heritability informativeness across all 34 matched cell system–trait comparisons after accounting for steady-state prioritization. Preserving perturbation-specific programs further yielded 2.5–5.3-fold higher trait relevance scores than programs derived from control cells, pooled perturbations or differential-expression summaries. In K562, Perturbscape-prioritized genes showed stronger enrichment for rare-variant burden genes than steady-state prioritization and were supported by orthogonal enhancer CRISPRi screens. In HepG2, LDL cholesterol-associated perturbation– induced programs specifically revealed statin-responsive pathways not significantly enriched by steady-state PoPS prioritization, supported by pharmacological transcriptional responses and population plasma proteomics. Perturbscape also recovered blood-related trait-conditioned trans-regulatory relationships that were specifically supported by population trans-eQTLs in IFN-γ-stimulated monocytes (OR = 1.30, P=1.6e-05). Perturbscape further revealed developmental-stage-specific convergence between monogenic diabetes regulators and polygenic T2D risk during pancreatic islet differentiation, and neuronal-subclass-specific autism-associated regulatory programs in vivo . Together, these findings establish perturbation-induced gene programs as a complementary layer of disease-relevant regulatory information, revealing genetically informative pathways and context-specific regulatory relationships incompletely represented by steady-state molecular atlases.

research.abstract: The family Noctuidae includes agricultural pests that vary in geographic distribution and host range. This study analyzed 30 mitogenomes representing 14 noctuid species; Ostrinia nubilalis (Crambidae) served as the phylogenetic outgroup. The genomes contained the typical complement of 37 mitochondrial genes and exhibited conserved gene order, pronounced A + T enrichment, and a preference for A/T-ending synonymous codons. A neutrality regression based on species means revealed a modest positive association between GC3 and GC12 (R 2 = 0.3201; p = 0.03494), although it could not distinguish the respective contributions of mutation and selection. Maximum-likelihood and Bayesian analyses of 13 protein-coding genes (11,229 bp) agreed on 26 of the 28 internal groupings in the maximum-likelihood tree, including a strongly supported Spodoptera clade. Differences in deeper relationships occurred at nodes with limited support. All 13 genes had dN/dS estimates below one (0.00306-0.01691), consistent with purifying selection. Codon usage varied among gene categories, and gene-wise codon bias was not significantly associated with dN/dS. Five crop-associated species with multiple larval host plants and documented long-distance migration- Helicoverpa armigera, Athetis lepigone, Spodoptera litura, S. frugiperda, and Mamestra brassicae -fell below the fitted neutrality regression line. Whether their ecological traits relate to this pattern remains requires broader taxonomic sampling and ecological data in future investigations.

research.abstract: SUMMARY The Columbretes archipelago in the Mediterranean is an example of deep isolation and sporadic human interaction during the Holocene. We recovered ancient DNA from 2,600-year-old microfauna and historical museum specimens to investigate the island’s extinct fauna. Despite challenging preservation conditions, we successfully recovered mitogenomes from historical Vipera latastei specimens, and partial mitogenomes from snake, skink, and lizard subfossils. Phylogenetic analyses confirm the extinct Columbretes snake as Vipera latastei , sharing a haplotype with the historical specimen and clustering with modern populations from northeastern Iberia, validating its provenance and suggesting a single mitochondrial lineage since isolation. The extinct skink, Chalcides bedriagai , also shows affinities with eastern Iberia. These results point to a vicariant origin for the herpetofauna, likely isolated on the island following sea level rise after the Last Glacial Maximum. Conversely, a 2,600-year-old mouse incisor yielded a Mus musculus mitogenome, indicating Iron Age human-mediated introduction. Additionally, genomic analysis of a 11th-century CE human burial revealed an individual with genetic affinities to the Central Mediterranean, highlighting medieval maritime mobility. This study resolves the long-debated Columbretes snake identity, traces biogeographic origins and illustrates the interplay of natural isolation and anthropogenic influence on the island biodiversity. GRAPHICAL ABSTRACT

research.abstract: Zoonotic tuberculosis (zTB), caused by animal-adapted members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), is classically attributed to M. bovis but is increasingly linked to M. orygis across South Asia. Species-level MTBC identification is rarely performed in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), leaving the zTB burden poorly defined. Bangladesh has endemic bovine tuberculosis, a growing dairy sector, unpasteurised-milk consumption, and expanding captive wildlife collections, yet the evidence has not been synthesised by diagnostic reliability. This systematic evidence map aimed to collate the evidence on zTB in Bangladesh and to review the diagnostic methods used to identify animal-adapted MTBC species, particularly M. bovis and M. orygis , in livestock, wildlife, and humans. Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Google Scholar, and BanglaJOL from the 1970s to June 2026; CAB Abstracts, Scopus, and Web of Science were not accessible. Two reviewers independently screened and appraised studies using the JBI checklist, assigning each to a five-level diagnostic evidence hierarchy (Level 1: WGS, phylogeny, RD typing, spoligotyping, or MLVA; Level 5: tuberculin skin test or serology only). These non-comparable tests precluded meta-analysis; therefore, findings are presented as an evidence map. Thirty-five studies met the inclusion criteria: 24 on prevalence in cattle/buffaloes, 10 on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in cattle, captive wildlife, and humans, and 1 specifically on molecular diagnosis and characterisation in humans. Most livestock studies used non-discriminatory tests (tuberculin skin tests, ELISA, or untyped PCR) and reported non-comparable reactor proportions of 1.2% to 33.7%. The few studies using species-level methods (Levels 1–2) confirmed M. orygis in cattle and in at least seven captive wildlife species, including monkeys, using marker-based molecular assays. Several historical reports of M. bovis were based on non-discriminatory PCR or serology, which cannot reliably distinguish among MTBC members. Human evidence was limited to three studies, including one WGS-confirmed M. orygis case identified through tuberculosis surveillance. In published reports from Bangladesh, M. orygis is the only animal-adapted MTBC member molecularly confirmed at the cattle–wildlife–human interface; existing M. bovis claims lack discriminatory support and require cautious reinterpretation. zTB surveillance should therefore move beyond an M. bovis -only framework and integrate species-level MTBC identification into a staged, resource-appropriate One Health strategy across animal, wildlife, and human health.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT The date palm is a high salinity tolerant fruit tree grown mainly in the region spanning from North Africa to parts of South Asia. Climate change models of this region indicate the possibility of increasing salinity in the future. The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is crucial for salinity tolerance in plants, serving as a primary defense mechanism by facilitating sodium exclusion. To better understand date palms’ salt tolerance, we analyzed variation in SOS pathway genes in a set of 197 date palm genomes collected from across the range of cultivation. Here, we show evidence for selective sweeps in multiple SOS pathway genes. A single major pdSOS1 haplotype is at very high frequency in Eastern and Western subpopulations, with a minor, likely ancestral haplotype still present in both geographical locations. Allele-specific gene expression analysis showed differences in salt-treated roots between swept and ancestral haplotypes. Interestingly, sequence-based analysis of the pdSOS1 haplotype suggested a second, much earlier introgression event between P. theophrasti and date palm, though direction is unclear. This event happened before both the selective sweep and the previously reported recent introgression to date palm. We identified a MITE transposable element inserted into a pdSOS1 intron on the swept haplotype, and a similar insertion was found in an intron of the SOS2 paralog pdCIPK8 . Both insertions are unique to date palm among Phoenix species. The pdCIPK8 haplotype containing the MITE is also at high frequency in both populations. Further analysis showed evidence for a selective sweep spanning the pdSOS3 region in the western population that shares similarity to an Eastern haplotype spanning the promoter region only. Slower extended haplotype homozygosity decay surrounding the genes in the western population suggests that the swept haplotype originated in the East and spread to the West in all cases. Altogether, our data provide evidence of selective sweeps in the date palm SOS pathway and may go to explaining how this species has developed such high salinity tolerance.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sputum culture conversion in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) is the most important interim indicator for drug-resistant (DR) tuberculosis (TB) treatment effectiveness. Bedaquiline-based regimens offer the possibility of more effective and less toxic treatment for DR TB. Bedaquiline-based regimens have been adopted as the new standard of care for DR TB, replacing the oto-and nephrotoxic aminoglycosides. We determined the median time to sputum culture conversion (TTCC) and associated factors among RR and MDR TB patients treated with Bedaquiline-based regimens, at Mulago National Referral Hospital, Uganda. METHODS: In a longitudinal type of observational study performed at Mulago Hospital, between January 2020 and June 2023, RR and MDR TB patients' records were reviewed to obtain data on socio-demographic and clinical factors, and TTCC. The study outcome was TTCC, recorded as time from RR/MDR TB treatment initiation to sputum culture conversion, which was defined as at least 2 consecutive negative TB sputum cultures, at least 30 days apart, for a RR/MDR PTB patient who was sputum culture positive at baseline. Analysis for median TTCC was done using Kaplan-Meier analysis, and the log-logistic parametric survival regression model was used to identify predictors for TTCC. RESULTS: Of the 265 participants, 196 (74.0%) were male, with median age of 35(IQR:27-42) years. The median TTCC was 7 (IQR:4-8) weeks from treatment initiation. Grade 2 + baseline smear positivity (adjusted Time Ratio (aTR):1.24, 95% CI:1.02-1.51, p = 0.029), grade 3 + baseline smear positivity (aTR:1.62, 95% CI:1.30-2.01, p < 0.001), cavitary disease on CXR (aTR:1.36, 95% CI:1.18-1.56, p < 0.001), and pleural effusion on CXR (aTR:1.81, 95% CI:1.43-2.31, p < 0.001) significantly prolonged the TTCC. Diabetes mellitus (7/265) significantly reduced the TTCC (aTR: 0.37, 95% CI: 0.22 - 0.60, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The WHO long regimen (9 months) was indistinguishable from the shorter 6-months regimen for the time to culture conversion. Integration of TB screening at points of care of high-risk patients like diabetics remains important for early detection and prompt initiation of DR TB treatment for better outcomes. The TB program and clinicians should enhance and individualize support for RR/MDR TB patients with more severe disease, to ensure optimum TTCC and successful treatment outcomes. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

research.abstract: Purpose Patients with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) complicated by Klebsiella pneumoniae (KP) pneumonia are prone to acute deterioration, frequently leading to intensive care unit (ICU) admission and higher mortality. This study aimed to identify independent risk factors for ICU admission among PTB patients with KP pneumonia and develop and internally validate a concise nomogram for early risk prediction. Patients and methods This single-center retrospective cohort study enrolled 102 PTB patients complicated by KP pneumonia (50 ICU group, 52 non-ICU group) at Public Health Clinical Center of Chengdu from June 2024 to June 2025. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression with 1000-bootstrap stability assessment was used to screen candidate variables. Firth penalized logistic regression was applied to identify independent risk factors and construct the nomogram. Internal validation was performed via 1000 bootstrap resampling. Multiple statistical approaches, including the area under the curve (AUC), calibration slope, Brier score, Hosmer-Lemeshow test, calibration plots, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curves (CIC), were adopted to quantify model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility. Results Screened by LASSO regression and further validated with Firth logistic regression, six-month pre-admission Gram-negative bacterial infection history, pre-admission carbapenem exposure within six months, respiratory virus infection, fungal infection, and systemic glucocorticoid use at admission constituted independent risk factors for ICU admission (all P). The nomogram had an apparent AUC of 0.935 and bootstrap-corrected AUC of 0.920 (optimism = 0.015), suggesting minimal overfitting within the development cohort, though external validation is needed to confirm generalizability. The apparent and optimism-corrected calibration slopes were 1.138 and 0.914, respectively. The apparent Brier score was 0.103, and the corrected Brier score was 0.083. The Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated favorable calibration (P=0.832). DCA and CIC confirmed stable clinical net benefit across reasonable threshold probabilities. Conclusion Constructed from five readily-available clinical variables, this nomogram shows good discrimination and satisfactory calibration for predicting ICU-admission risk in PTB patients with KP pneumonia. External validation is still needed to verify its generalizability. Before such validation is performed, the tool should serve only as a supportive risk-stratification aid instead of a standalone clinical decision-making instrument. It may help identify patients who deserve intensified monitoring owing to high risk of clinical deterioration.

research.abstract: Background: Restrictions on the types of food available on land have repeatedly triggered the convergent evolution of herbivory in terrestrial animals. This pattern also holds true in many terrestrially adapted crabs, which have independently colonized land more than 17 times since the Cretaceous. Many clades of terrestrial crabs are now almost completely herbivorous, standing in contrast to the ancestral pattern of detrivory. While many bacteria possess efficient pathways for degrading lignin and cellulose, the role of gut microbiomes in facilitating these dietary shifts in terrestrial crabs remains poorly understood. To explore the relationship between microbial community structure and the ability of land crabs to digest lignocellulose, we conducted read-based and assembly-based metagenomic analyses on feces collected from the guts of 14 crab species across six genera, representing a gradient of terrestriality from the lower intertidal zone to forested habitats. Results: We generated 129 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) that represent key members of these gut microbial communities, establishing a foundational resource for future studies on crab-microbiome interactions. We found that host genus explained most of the variation in bacterial community composition, while degree of terrestrial adaptation (i.e. terrestrial grade) explained a smaller proportion. We also identified multiple bacterial genera that strikingly differed in relative abundance across terrestrial grades, crab genera, and diet type. Broad-scale functional analyses of general carbon metabolism across crabs revealed an absence of complete pathways in crabs from lower terrestrial grades, suggesting a functional divergence in gut communities linked to habitat transition. Fine-scale functional analyses of predicted carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZyme) domains allowed us to connect specific MAGs to lignocellulose degradation pathway genes, demonstrating that different crab genera harbor distinct microbial taxa that may have similar CAZyme profiles in their guts. Conclusions: This work provides a foundational metagenomic resource for genomic exploration of microbial communities in terrestrial crab guts. These results suggest that the gut microbiomes of terrestrially adapted crabs are structured primarily by host identity and may have convergently acquired microbes with similar functions to help perform lignocellulose degradation. Overall, different degrees of adaptation to terrestrial environments, including resulting dietary shifts, may be responsible for functional divergence in crab gut community assembly.

research.abstract: Abstract Whole-genome alignments are fundamental resources in comparative genomics, because they place genes and their surrounding sequences in a shared evolutionary context. Progressive Cactus aligns large numbers of genomes without a reference genome and reconstructs ancestral sequences along the input phylogeny. However, its Hierarchical Alignment Format output has mainly been used for visualization, phylogenomics, and pangenome studies, and gene-level analyses of these alignments remain difficult. Here, we present Genomes2Genes, a pipeline that converts Progressive Cactus graph-based alignments into validated coding sequence alignments of extant species and their reconstructed ancestors. The pipeline extracts exon alignment blocks, handles atypical genomic jumps, stitches exons into transcripts, and reports start codons, stop codons, and frameshifting indels across species, with validation steps throughout and a base-by-base audit of the final alignments. It catches both biological and technical artifacts and can be run on any part of the genome. We anticipate that this pipeline will be useful in identifying and removing problematic regions used in the potential reconstruction of species or gene phylogenies. We developed and tested the pipeline on a whole-genome alignment of 21 Brassicaceae species and 2 outgroups and found that, among 45,491 lineage-specific genes, the pipeline supported 22,376 candidate de novo genes, of which 1,811 had complete evidence of enabler mutations. Genomes2Genes is publicly available and extends whole-genome alignments to gene-level questions in comparative genomics and evolutionary biology.

Here we resolve the phylogenomic timescale, molecular adaptation, and agricultural demography of Phylum Nematoda across 544 verified NCBI sequence records (plus 956 slices quarantined by bio-suite-seqnet). Our dataset combines a 64-species, 18-locus supermatrix (L = 146,840 aligned columns spanning Clade I virus vectors, Clade IVa pine-wilt Aphelenchoidea, and Clade IVb Tylenchomorpha crop pests rooted on Chromadorea outgroups) with 48 nuclear functional coding sequences and 12 demographic cohorts (432 pest isolates). research.abstract: Abstract The Wnt gene family plays a central role in vertebrate development, yet its evolutionary dynamics across lineages remain largely unexplored. Here, we present the most comprehensive analysis of Wnt gene evolution in vertebrates to date, leveraging a large-scale comparative genomics approach of 38,886 Wnt gene sequences mined from 1,961 species. We first investigate overall patterns of gene retention, duplication, and loss, and then focus specifically on the impact of whole-genome duplications (WGDs). We uncover striking variation in Wnt gene repertoire sizes, with ray-finned fishes (Actinopterygii) exhibiting the largest repertoires – even after excluding taxa with recent WGDs. Notably, we identify extreme expansions in polyploid cyprinids, including an octoploid hybrid harbouring 99 Wnt genes, the highest number observed. Unexpectedly elevated Wnt copy numbers in diploid species, such as in the Antarctic lanternfish (Electrona antarctica) and the brook lamprey (Lethenteron reissneri), point to lineage-specific expansions, although the potential adaptive significance of these expansions remains to be tested. Evolutionary rate analyses reveal that certain Wnt clades – especially Wnt8 and Wnt16 – exhibit elevated dN/dS ratios and high birth–death rates, consistent with repeated episodes of relaxed constraint and/or adaptive diversification. Contrary to our expectations, there was no relationship between developmental expression timing and evolutionary rates, suggesting pleiotropic regulation and functional redundancy of Wnt genes. Altogether, our findings reveal widespread variation in Wnt copy number and turnover among lineages, shaped by both genome duplication history and divergent evolutionary trajectories. This work provides a high-resolution framework for understanding the molecular evolution of a key developmental toolkit and highlights candidate genes for future studies of vertebrate eco-morphological diversity.

research.abstract: Abstract Complex genomic rearrangements (CGRs) are hallmarks of tumor genomes, yet their architectures and origins remain poorly understood. We utilized optical mapping to profile the genomic landscapes of lung tissues across various stages - from normal and benign lesions to advanced carcinomas - to characterize genome disorganization during carcinogenesis. We developed omcplR to resolve the CGR architectures and predict their genesis using the genome-graph framework. Our findings reveal that many CGRs arise from hierarchical combinations of localized structural variations that are unlikely due to break-fusion-bridge, chromothripsis, or chromoplexy. We termed this process chromodiadochi: a cascade of nested rearrangements accumulating over multiple generations during carcinogenesis. Early intra-chromosomal junctions in CGRs typically localized within specific chromatin domains, while late junctions in advanced tumors occurred in more heterogeneous contexts and showed signs of positive selection. A composite signature of genomic alterations, including the CGRs, captures the trajectory of progressive genomic structural disorganization and instability from benign tissue to malignancy.

research.abstract: INTRODUCTION: TB (tuberculosis) due to Mycobacterium tuberculosis continues to be a significant worldwide health issue. Timely and reliable diagnostic tests will improve treatment outcomes and reduce the spread of disease. Traditional TB diagnostics currently available, such as smear microscopy and culture, have significant limitations with regard to sensitivity and turnaround times, especially for smear-negative cases and for tuberculosis in extrapulmonary locations. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this review is to analyze the evolution of TB diagnostics from traditional microbiology to new molecular diagnostic methods (including CRISPR, biosensor technology, and microfluidic methods), including an assessment of their diagnostic testing performance, feasibility, and potential for the future. METHODS: The systematic narrative review aimed to systematically assess literature published from 2020 to 2025 retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. The review was carried out according to the PRISMA guidelines and included 89 studies after screening and assessing for eligibility. The data were analysed qualitatively (i.e., through thematic analysis) by comparing data from conventional, molecular, and next-generation diagnostic methods. RESULTS: Molecular tests (e.g., GeneXpert, Line Probe Assays, PCR, and Whole Genome Sequencing) provide greater sensitivity and specificity than traditional methods and allow for faster diagnosis. Additionally, newer CRISPR-based tests, biosensors, and microfluidic devices hold promise for rapid, portable, point-of-care diagnosis of tuberculosis. DISCUSSION: The findings indicate that molecular diagnostics improve rapid detection and drug-resistance profiling, while CRISPR and biosensor platforms offer potential for rapid point-of-care testing. However, affordability, infrastructure, clinical validation, and scalability remain important barriers. CONCLUSION: The use of molecular diagnostic testing, CRISPR technology, biosensors, artificial intelligence, and portable platforms will dramatically enhance existing TB surveillance systems and strategies for controlling the disease globally.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , remains a major global health challenge, further exacerbated by the rapid emergence of drug-resistant strains. Despite continuous efforts, the discovery of novel anti-TB agents has lagged behind the evolution of resistance, largely due to the limitations of conventional experimental pipelines and the growing biological complexity of the pathogen. In recent years, computational drug discovery approaches—including virtual screening, artificial intelligence (AI)-driven modeling, and hybrid computational frameworks—have substantially expanded the chemical space accessible for early-stage anti-TB research. However, their translational success remains limited. This discrepancy reflects a fundamental mismatch between target-centric computational paradigms and the multi-scale biological constraints of Mtb , including permeability barriers, efflux mechanisms, metabolic state heterogeneity, lesion-level pharmacokinetics, and regimen-dependent therapeutic effects. This review critically evaluates current computational strategies for anti-TB drug screening, with particular emphasis on their performance under TB-specific biological and resistance constraints. We further explore computational approaches designed to address drug-resistant Mtb , including resistance-aware compound design, host-directed therapy, and combination regimen modeling. Finally, we explore key limitations in current computational pipelines, including challenges in data quality, biological integration, and regimen-level modeling, and propose a shift toward biologically grounded, regimen-aware, and systems-level frameworks. Bridging the gap between in silico prediction and clinical efficacy will require integrating multi-scale biological realism into computational pipelines, enabling more reliable translation of computational advances into effective anti-TB therapeutics.

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

research.abstract: Risk of pregnancy complications is reassessed at each antenatal visit, but whether earlier predictions add information beyond the most recent one is unclear. Classifying every prediction as low or high risk can leave uncertainty unexpressed. Whether reliability per visit holds across visits is also unclear. This secondary analysis included 9289 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort (eight US centres, 2010-2013). Logistic regression models predicted gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, suspected fetal growth restriction and large for gestational age at 6-13, 16-21 and 22-29 weeks (Visits 3). Mondrian conformal prediction reported 'no' (low risk), 'yes' (high risk), or both (review). To test whether prediction history adds information beyond the Visit 3 prediction, we compared, among women classified as high risk at Visit 3, those first classified as high risk at Visit 2 or 3 (emerging high) with those classified as high risk at all three visits (persistent high), adjusting for Visit 3 predicted probability. The adjusted proportion with the outcome was higher in the emerging-high than the persistent-high group, by 6.1 percentage points for large for gestational age (95% CI -0.4 to 12.2) and 3.8 percentage points for suspected fetal growth restriction (-0.9 to 8.1). Other outcomes showed adjusted differences close to zero. With conformal prediction calibrated to a 90% level at each visit, the reported answers included the actual outcome in 89.6-90.6% of women at each visit (coverage). Coverage decreased when each woman's three visits were considered together (79.0-85.4%). For fetal growth outcomes, how a woman's predicted risk evolved during pregnancy may add information beyond her Visit 3 prediction. For repeated clinical use, the target coverage level should reflect the acceptable risk of incorrect low- or high-risk classifications over a woman's follow-up and the clinical decisions supported at each visit.

research.abstract: Abstract Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.

research.abstract: Coupled Metropolis-Hastings MCMC sampling (runie-mcmc-skyline: G = 10,000 generations, 20% burn-in = 2,000 discarded, 8,000 posterior states) across 64 ancient/modern hominin mitogenomes and 16 nuclear loci (L = 87,227 *MAFFT / 86,612 Native Rust gotoh-msa aligned bp) resolving the 5-stage Neanderthal Ne(t) collapse (13,893 to 602.7 at 39.2 ka BP) and 37.3x speedup over *MAFFT + *IQ-TREE + *BEAST v1.10.4 Reconstructing the demographic trajectory and extinction timing of archaic hominins from ancient DNA requires separating genuine coalescent bottlenecks from post-mortem cytosine deamination and nuclear pseudogene artifacts while jointly estimating tree topology, divergence dates, and effective population size over time. Here we introduce and validate a configurable long-form Bayesian Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler inside the Rust Native Inference Engine (runie-mcmc-skyline; default 10,000 generations with a 20% burn-in gate) and benchmark it against *BEAST, *IQ-TREE with *LSD2, and *PAML codeml across an 87,227-bp hominin alignment spanning Neanderthals, Denisovans, Sima de los Huesos, and modern humans. Sampling the stationary posterior distribution reconstructs a five-stage Neanderthal demographic collapse from a Middle Pleistocene effective population size of 13,893 down to 603 breeding individuals at the 39.2 ka extinction horizon, driven by recurring glacial bottlenecks, consanguineous inbreeding, and a three-fold relaxation of mitochondrial purifying selection. Finally, stage-level timing comparisons demonstrate that Native Rust completes alignment and 10,000-generation MCMC sampling 37.3-fold faster than the external *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE, and *BEAST tool chain while preventing the 22.3-fold false terminal population inflation caused by uncleaned ancient-DNA deamination. research.abstract: Phylogenetic trees are hybrid objects: branch lengths vary continuously, while topologies change discretely through edge contractions and expansions. Billera-Holmes-Vogtmann (BHV) tree space provides a canonical geometry for this structure, representing each resolved topology as a Euclidean orthant and topological changes as motion across shared lower-dimensional boundaries. We introduce PhylaFlow, a hybrid flow-matching model that learns posterior-basin transport in BHV tree space. PhylaFlow is trained on BHV geodesic paths from random starting trees to short-run posterior samples, coupling continuous branch-length motion within orthants with learned boundary events and discrete topology transitions. We evaluate the learned geometry operationally: if the flow reaches posterior-relevant regions, finite-budget Bayesian refinement initialized from, or guided by, its terminal trees should recover posterior-supported topologies more efficiently. Across DS1-DS8 phylogenetic posterior benchmarks, PhylaFlow substantially reduces initial Tree-KL relative to classical initializers. After finite-budget MrBayes refinement, direct PhylaFlow improves early and intermediate topology-recovery trajectories on most datasets, while split-guided PhylaFlow-MCMC obtains the strongest hard-case results. The best PhylaFlow variant outperforms short-warmup on seven of eight datasets and PhyloGFN on five of eight under the same refinement budget. In a joint sequence-conditioned experiment, sequence embeddings steer posterior split recovery, although exact posterior topology recovery remains preliminary. These results show that hybrid flow matching can learn actionable transport in BHV tree space and provide a geometry-aware proposal mechanism for Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

research.abstract: Abstract A longstanding goal in human genetics is to prioritize noncoding loci that, when disrupted, lead to developmental disorders and other Mendelian traits. In pursuit of this goal, multiple metrics have been developed to distinguish neutrally evolving sequences from those subjected to purifying selection. These metrics are commonly evaluated genome-wide, e.g., by computing a precision-recall curve on windows tiling the entire noncoding genome. Here, we identify parts of the noncoding genome where these metrics are distorted due to “bias” in the underlying models of neutral genetic variation and underperform due to a low “signal-to-noise ratio” in the genetic data. The most extreme effects are found for Gnocchi (Chen et al. 2024), the performance of which declines as GC content increases. We trace the source of the bias in Gnocchi to a mismatch between the training set of de novo mutations (DNMs) used to adjust expected SNP counts and the genomic windows on which those expected counts are computed. Resolving that mismatch produces a more calibrated version of Gnocchi, significantly improving its interpretability in applications. Looking forward, we suggest annotating constraint scores of noncoding genomic intervals with robust measures of the bias of the corresponding model, allowing users to gauge confidence in those scores.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Brain-predicted age, estimated from structural MRI data, is a machine-learning biomarker of biological brain aging. Greater brain age gap (BAG) indicates advanced brain aging and is associated with cognitive decline and mortality. Cardiometabolic risk factors, including elevated blood glucose, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, and cholesterol, increase risk of cognitive impairment and dementia in aging. Their relationship with BAG in severe obesity remains poorly characterized despite increased prevalence of cardiometabolic risk factors among this population. Methods T1-weighted MRI data from 97 adults (BMI 35-73) were used to calculate BAG using ENIGMA and Pyment brain age models. Associations between BAG and HbA1c, BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were examined using multiple linear regression and MM–estimation robust regression, adjusting for age, sex, and race. Post hoc analyses stratified models by clinical HbA1c cutoffs (normoglycemic, prediabetic, diabetic). Results Higher HbA1c was associated with greater BAG ENIGMA ( B = 1.58, p = .014) and BAG Pyment ( B = 0.93, p = .013) in linear regression models. In robust models, HbA1c remained significantly associated with BAG ENIGMA ( B = 1.70, p = .002) but not BAG Pyment ( B = 0.71, p = .13). BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia were not associated with BAG in either linear or robust models. HbA1c was associated with greater BAG ENIGMA ( B = 2.15, p = .01) and BAG Pyment ( B =1.21, p = .04) in those at or above prediabetic levels and with BAG ENIGMA ( B = 2.49, p = .047) in those with diabetes. Conclusions Elevated HbA1c is associated with advanced brain aging in individuals with severe obesity. BAG was not associated with BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia, which may reflect the restricted BMI range inherent to the sample with severe obesity. HIGHLIGHTS Elevated HbA1c was associated with advanced brain aging in individuals with severe obesity. HbA1c-BAG associations were seen primarily in the context of clinically elevated levels (i.e. prediabetes and diabetes). The study did not provide evidence to support that BMI, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia are associated with BAG in individuals with severe obesity ENIGMA and Pyment models showed limited agreement in BAG estimates in a sample of individuals with severe obesity.

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

items.summary: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. research.journal: European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

items.title: Genomic analysis of the Streptococcus anginosus group; taxonomic implications, evolutionary insights and clinical considerations

research.abstract: Abstract Background The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) ( S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus ) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group’s diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa ( S. anginosus , S. hominis , S. whileyi and S. vaginalis ). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex- S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ∼15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity ( S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi ) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.
