research.abstract: Abstract Sex-determining systems in flatfishes are highly diverse, and even closely related species can differ in both sex-determining loci and heterogametic systems. In common dab ( Limanda limanda ), the genetic basis of sex determination has not yet been established. Here, we investigated sex determination using pooled whole-genome sequencing combined with long-read genome sequencing of females and males from Iceland and Norway. Genome-wide allele-frequency analyses identified sex-associated regions consistent with male heterogamety (XX/XY), with the strongest signal on chromosome 16. Comparison of the existing reference assembly, which represents an X haplotype at this locus, with a haplotype-resolved male PacBio HiFi assembly revealed a ∼21.5 kb Y-specific insertion on chromosome 16. The insertion showed complete coverage in male pools but little or no coverage in female pools from either population. It contained a translocated genomic segment including a copy of gonadal soma-derived factor ( gsdf ) and a predicted gene of unknown function. Comparative genomic analyses were consistent with this segment originating from an autosomal gsdf -containing region on chromosome 1. Given the recurrent recruitment of gsdf as a sex-determining factor in teleosts, we designate the Y-linked copy gsdfY and identify it as the strongest candidate for the master sex-determining gene in common dab. Additional broad sex-associated differentiation on chromosome 19 was restricted to the Icelandic samples and may reflect population-specific expansion of the sex-linked region, although its structural basis remains unresolved. Together, these findings provide the first genomic characterization of sex determination in common dab and demonstrate how gene duplication and translocation can contribute to the evolution of novel sex-determining systems in flatfishes.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

authors.name: van de Wouw, Y. A. J.
van de Werken, H. J. G.

research.abstract: Background: Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a metastatic, heterogeneous malignancy accounting for 2-5% of cancer diagnoses globally. Failure to identify the primary site precludes tumor-type-specific therapy and, together with an aggressive clinical course, contributes to poor survival. The biological mechanisms driving these behaviors remain poorly understood. A deeper understanding of CUP biology is therefore essential to improve diagnostic precision and therapeutic strategies. To address this knowledge gap, we comprehensively characterized the multi-omics landscape of CUP and identified biological and potentially therapeutic targets beyond tissue-of-origin (ToO) assignment. Methods: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 283 CUP patients were analyzed for ToO predictions, mutational signatures, driver alterations, genetic immune escape (GIE), and clinically actionable alterations. Matched RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) data from 79 cases were used to characterize functional gene expression signatures and define transcriptomic subtypes. Clinical, WGS, and RNA-seq data were integrated via weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). Results: High-confidence ToO predictions (likelihood >80%) were obtained for 58% of CUPs, most commonly predicting lung, gastrointestinal, and biliary tract origins. Mutational signatures clustering revealed four subgroups dominated by tobacco smoking, defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR), UV exposure, and APOBEC activity, while a fifth group, comprising most tumors (n=169; 60%), showed mixed mutational processes. The cohort also frequently exhibited mutations in established cancer driver genes, including TP53, CDKN2A, KRAS, and epigenetic modifiers ARID1A, SMARCA4, and ARID2. GIE alterations occurred in 35% of tumors, mostly involving HLA-I genes. Transcriptomic profiling defined five subtypes with different degrees of immune infiltration, fibrosis, and tumor proliferation. These subtypes were not significantly associated with clinical or genomic features, indicating that the tumor microenvironment (TME) represents another layer of CUP heterogeneity. WGCNA further linked proliferative programs to cell-cycle, DNA-replication, and neuroendocrine features. WGS data identified potentially targetable alterations in 64% of the CUP patients. Conclusions: CUP comprises biologically heterogeneous tumors with diverse predicted origins, mutational histories, and TME subtypes. Transcriptomic profiling and integrated genomics suggest that immune escape and rapid proliferation contribute to the clinical aggressive behavior. Together, these findings provide a molecular framework for understanding CUP heterogeneity and support therapeutic stratification by both ToO predictions and tumor-specific molecular alterations.

research.abstract: Introduction Abutilon fruticosum Guill. & Perr. is a drought-tolerant Malvaceae subshrub native to Saudi Arabia. However, no mitochondrial genome has previously been reported for the genus Abutilon . This study reports the first complete mitochondrial genome of A. fruticosum and evaluates its comparative and phylogenetic relationships within Malvaceae. Methods The mitochondrial genome was assembled, annotated, and analyzed for genome composition, repetitive sequences, codon usage, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, synonymous and nonsynonymous substitution rates, collinearity, and phylogenetic relationships inferred from 32 shared mitochondrial protein-coding genes across ten taxa. Results The mitogenome was assembled as a circular molecule of 826,313 bp, with a GC content of 44.94%, and contained 37 protein-coding genes, 3 rRNA genes, and 21 tRNA genes. Comparative analyses of five Malvaceae mitogenomes revealed conserved codon-usage patterns, with weak-to-moderate bias influenced by nucleotide composition and functional constraints, but substantial variation in repeat abundance and distribution. DeepredMT predicted 397 RNA-editing sites in A. fruticosum , fewer than in Tilia amurensis , Gossypium trilobum , and Hibiscus cannabinus , but slightly more than in Adansonia perrieri . Simple sequence repeats and short dispersed repeats predominated, whereas G. trilobum had the greatest proportion of long repeats and H. cannabinus the highest repeat density. Nucleotide-diversity hotspots were detected in rpl16 , rps3 , cox2 , and rpl2 , while most protein-coding genes had dN/dS values below 1. The elevated dN/dS signal in rps4 suggested accelerated evolution or relaxed functional constraint, warranting further investigation. Maximum-likelihood analysis recovered A. fruticosum (tribe Malveae) as sister to the sampled Hibiscus – Gossypium clade with strong support. Discussion This study presents the first mitochondrial genome of Abutilon , expanding mitogenomic resources for Malvaceae. The A. fruticosum mitogenome shows conserved gene content and codon usage, alongside lineage-specific variation in repeat organization, predicted RNA-editing sites, nucleotide diversity, and localized sequence divergence. The phylogenetic placement is consistent with the accepted classification of A. fruticosum in Malvoideae and illustrates the potential of mitogenomic data for systematic studies within Malvaceae, although broader taxon sampling is needed to test this placement. This mitogenome provides a resource for marker development, population-genetic studies, comparative mitogenomics, and phylogenetic research on Abutilon and related Malvaceae lineages.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: Rationale: Point of care lung ultrasound is portable and radiation free and could extend tuberculosis screening to settings without chest radiography, but no standardized criteria exist for interpreting it for tuberculosis. Objectives: To develop and internally evaluate deep learning models that classify pulmonary tuberculosis from lung ultrasound images, alone and combined with routine clinical variables, and to derive an abbreviated scanning protocol. Methods: In a prospective study in Kampala, Uganda (2023 to 2025), we enrolled people aged 13 years or older with microbiologically confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis, their household contacts, and symptomatic people with other respiratory conditions. One still frame from each of 12 lung ultrasound zones was analyzed with an attention-based multiple-instance learning network. We compared clinical-only (random forest), ultrasound only, and combined models and derived a 6 zone protocol from training set attention weights. Participants were allocated to training (n = 223), validation (n = 20), and held-out test (n = 73) sets. Results: Of 318 enrolled participants, 316 were analyzed (118 with and 198 without tuberculosis). In the test set, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80 to 0.95) for the clinical-only model; 0.93 (0.86 to 0.97) and 0.95 (0.89 to 0.99) for the 12 zone ultrasound-only and combined models; and 0.91 (0.83 to 0.97) and 0.93 (0.86 to 0.99) for the corresponding 6-zone models. At 90% sensitivity, specificity was 82.2% (34.9 to 97.8) for the 12-zone combined model and 91.1% (25.0 to 98.0) for the 6-zone combined model. Point estimates for all 12-zone models and the 6-zone combined model met the 2025 World Health Organization minimum accuracy targets for a high-sensitivity screening test ([≥]90% sensitivity, [≥]60% specificity). Conclusion: Lung ultrasound analyzed with attention-based deep learning and combined with clinical variables showed high internal discrimination for pulmonary tuberculosis, and a simplified 6-zone protocol retained most of this performance. External validation in intended-use screening populations is needed

research.abstract: Evaluating a 64-Species, 18-Locus Total-Evidence Supermatrix (L = 31,111 Aligned Columns; 11,436,768 Quartets), 48 Nuclear Functional CDS Orthologs, and 12 Single-Species Regional and Multi-Locus NCBI PopSet Cohorts (N = 432 Isolates) Exclusively via Constrained 100% Native Rust Bio-Suite Combinatorial Optimization (B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC Generations) We reconstruct the Jurassic-to-Anthropocene global radiation, vector-host co-evolution, and historical demographic dynamics of Anopheles malaria mosquitoes across 544 verified NCBI sequence records comprising a 64-species, 18-locus supermatrix (L = 31,111 aligned columns), 48 nuclear functional coding sequences, and 12 single-species regional and multi-locus NCBI PopSet cohorts (12 × N = 36 = 432 isolates). Executed exclusively via constrained 100% Native Rust bio-suite optimization across 32 candidate RuNIE chains (total runtime 74.48 s; B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC generations with 20% burn-in), RY3 purine/pyrimidine recoding under GTR+F+R4 reduces Dipteran AT-bias heterogeneity by 84.4% (RCFV = 0.0024 vs. 0.0154, ln L = -339,400.67), dating Crown Culicidae to 194.8 Ma, Crown Anophelinae to 108.4 Ma, the Gondwanan Nyssorhynchus–Cellia split to 78.9 Ma, and the African Gambiae Complex to 4.62 Ma. Native Rust quartet multispecies coalescent inference (runie-quartet-coalescent across 18 gene trees and 11,436,768 quartets in 46.97 ms) resolves 7,414,073 satisfied quartets (normalized Q = 0.6483, mean LPP = 0.8477) while ABBA-BABA tests confirm porous An. gambiae–coluzzii–arabiensis introgression (D = +0.4359 to +0.5177, Z = 12.11–13.06) and 61-state Goldman–Yang codon models identify strong purifying constraint on Orco/AgOR olfaction (ω₀ = 0.056) alongside diversifying selection on TEP1/LRIM1 immunity (ω₂ = 3.23), Anophelin/D7 saliva (ω₂ = 2.66), and VGSC/ACE1/GSTe2 resistance (ω₂ = 2.91). Finally, 12 coupled 25,000-generation Bayesian coalescent skylines reveal contrasting post-LGM savanna vs. Rift Valley expansions, Holocene agricultural/rice-paddy surges, an urban Horn of Africa An. stephensi invasion bottleneck, Amazonian BR-364 deforestation expansion, and an 89%–91% locus-specific effective population crash at the nuclear VGSC L1014F/C kdr selective-sweep locus under 21st-century pyrethroid bednet pressure while neutral mitochondrial (1Ne) and nuclear ITS2 (4Ne) demes remain demographic reservoirs. research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

research.abstract: Summary Two otherwise healthy patients from Colombia, now aged 30 and 38 years, developed pulmonary tuberculosis due to inherited, complete TNF deficiency at the ages of 19 and 18 years. We report here a previously healthy Iranian patient with inherited complete TNF deficiency who was diagnosed with both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB between 10 and 15 years of age. The homozygous TNF variant (c.673C>T) introduces a premature stop codon (TNF p.Q225*) resulting in losses of expression and function. Despite normal myeloid and lymphoid subset development, the patient’s primary leukocytes do not secrete detectable amounts of TNF. As in the TNF-deficient Colombian patients, the respiratory burst of GM-CSF-derived macrophages is impaired. Our findings expand the spectrum of TB phenotypes in patients with TNF deficiency and confirm that TNF is essential for immunity to M. tuberculosis in humans but apparently redundant against many other pathogens, including weakly virulent mycobacteria.

research.abstract: Tetrigidae is an early-branching family of Caelifera whose species live on damp ground, feed largely on mosses, algae and detritus, and often show wing and pronotum polymorphism. Which chemosensory and detoxification genes underlie this lifestyle is unknown. We generated an Oxford Nanopore PCR-cDNA transcriptome from a pooled sample of adult Hyboella guangxiensis (4.25 million full-length reads) and used it, together with protein homology, to filter the 17,996 machine-learning gene models of its chromosome-level genome to 15,338 supported genes without loss of BUSCO completeness. For nine families (OBP, CSP, IR, SNMP, P450, CCE, GST, UGT, ABC), full-length transcripts corrected 28 of 447 loci, including split and fused models, and brought protein lengths into agreement with orthologs of the sister species Bolivaritettix circocephalus (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.00066). Only 251 loci were supported by complete-ORF transcripts, and 101 had no full-length reads at all. Reconciliation of family phylogenies across eleven orthopteran genomes assigned 119 well-supported duplications to the Tetrigidae stem branch, dominated by P450 (42), UGT (27) and ABC (22) genes, and identified 63 homologous groups restricted to Tetrigidae. Five lineage-specific groups detected as transcripts in adults were validated at the genome level in four non-tetrigid outgroups: a CYP301A-like array, a Tetrigidae-specific UGT clade, two Tetrigidae-specific chemosensory proteins, a CYP9E2-like array and an esterase FE4-like array. Branch-site tests found episodic selection on some members of the UGT and CYP301A-like groups and in 7 of 28 recent paralog pairs, but not in the CYP9E2-like, FE4-like or CSP groups. These genes are candidates for the cuticular, chemosensory and dietary adaptations of pygmy grasshoppers to be tested with tissue-resolved data, whereas no family member could be linked to wing polymorphism.

To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally…

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. Results We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846–0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful. Availability Code is available at SAGE-Lab-UMass/Big-TB-benchmark; data are available at figshare. Contact [email removed] Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

items.title: Natural selection on synonymous genetic variation in the major histocompatibility complex
items.summary: Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. research.abstract: Abstract Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural selection on synonymous variation in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a highly polymorphic multigene locus that plays a crucial role in pathogen recognition by the adaptive immune system of vertebrate species. Using data from a wild population of Great Reed Warblers, I show that codon usage in exon 3 of MHC class I (MHC-I) genes is under strong purifying selection in 57 out of 87 codon sites. Scanning the Great Reed Warbler genome for tRNA genes revealed that, for most amino acids, bias towards preferred codons was associated with abundances of tRNA isotypes, indicating that the purifying selection is likely driven by selection for increased translational efficiency. However, spikes of synonymous variation appeared in 30 of the 87 sites in the MHC-I exon 3, and in those sites, codon usage bias and correlations with tRNA abundances were reduced. About half of these sites fall in CpG contexts, where cytosine deamination elevates the mutation rate; the other half do not, leaving the driver of much of the variation unexplained. The distribution of the spikes of synonymous variation showed no consistent association with structural domains of the MHC-I protein, nor with sites under positive selection for amino acid change, which are considered important for antigen binding properties. Intriguingly, the amount of synonymous variation in genotypes showed a positive correlation with Darwinian fitness, indicating that important evolutionary forces are at play that neutralize purifying selection in the 30 sites. From an ultimate perspective, the release of purifying selection among certain sites in MHC genes may indicate an arms race with pathogens, and I propose that the spikes of synonymous variation reveal a footprint of natural selection to escape inhibitory molecular interactions targeting MHC mRNA. I advance this RNA-level arms race as a novel axis of host–pathogen coevolution and a hypothesis to be tested directly. The fitness association is specific to synonymous variation, independent of amino-acid differences and the number of MHC alleles in genotypes, implicating selection on the synonymous variation itself rather than linked protein-level diversity. These results expose a previously unrecognized layer of selection in a key immune gene family and highlight the potential functional importance of synonymous variation in host–pathogen coevolution with direct implications for understanding susceptibility to infectious diseases. Significance Statement Roughly a quarter of DNA mutations carry no amino acid change, yet a growing body of evidence shows such synonymous variation can still shape how genes work. This study shows that genes of the major histocompatibility complex, central to how vertebrates detect infection, carry a hidden layer of natural selection acting on this synonymous variation, and that it is linked to individual fitness in a wild bird population. The findings suggest hosts and pathogens may be locked in an evolutionary arms race playing out beneath the level of protein sequence, with implications for how susceptibility to infectious disease is understood and studied.

research.abstract: Abstract Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ∼2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic, and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo, and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (∼14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/ Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.

items.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes

research.abstract: Abstract Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda . The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

items.title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
items.summary: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of a country’s tuberculosis burden while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports. IMPORTANCE Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing is essential for tracking outbreaks and directing limited public health resources. The decades-old laboratory method for spoligotyping, a widely used genetic fingerprint for this bacterium, is slow, labor-intensive, and hard to read. Newer sequencing-based approaches solve these problems but usually still need an expensive, time-consuming commercial kit to prepare samples for sequencing. This work describes HiSpoT, a simplified, low-cost, one-tube method that prepares samples for sequencing without a commercial kit, cutting turnaround from about a week to about two days while testing many samples together. Because HiSpoT results agree with results obtained from older typing methods, laboratories anywhere with basic sequencing equipment can compare results to decades of stored international data. Two free, open-source computer programs are also provided so laboratories with limited bioinformatics expertise can analyze their sequencing data automatically.

items.title: Do divergent mitochondrial backgrounds alter the fate of nuclear alleles during hybridization and admixture?
items.summary: Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential…

research.abstract: Abstract Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential “hot-spots” for hybrid incompatibilities. Here, we test whether selection against mitonuclear incompatibilities drives repeatable hybridization outcomes. Specifically, we experimentally evolved three sets of five populations of hybrid Drosophila melanogaster , each carrying the same nuclear chromosomes but paired with one of three increasingly divergent mitochondrial DNA backgrounds. We hypothesized that accumulated incompatibilities would result in different patterns of nuclear admixture among mitochondrial backgrounds. To test this, we tracked nuclear allele frequencies in all 15 populations by whole-genome sequencing at intermediate time points. After 25 generations, we observed that rapid genomic evolution produced a strikingly parallel mosaic of both nuclear ancestries, independent of mitochondrial background. Contrary to our hypothesis, we found no evidence that mitochondrial background shaped nuclear admixture, even for interspecific combinations. These results suggest that in species with large effective population sizes, efficient purifying selection limits the accumulation of mitonuclear incompatibilities, allowing selection on nuclear alleles to promote repeatable ancestry sorting immediately following hybridization.

items.title: Effect of starting metformin on severe and long COVID-19 among people living with type 2 diabetes in England: a new user cohort study in OpenSAFELY-TPP
items.summary: IntroductionObservational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls. Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect. No large observational study has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in…

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Observational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls. Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect. No large observational study has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We aimed to estimate this effect on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID among adults with T2D in England. Research design and methods Using OpenSAFELY-TPP linked NHS electronic health records, we conducted a population-based cohort study with a landmark new-user design. Adults aged 18-85 years newly diagnosed with T2D (August 2018-August 2019) were classified as starting metformin monotherapy within 6 months or not starting any antidiabetic drug, based on prescription data. Follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis and before the UK pandemic (avoiding immortal time) for up to 2 years. We estimated intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects using weighted Cox and pooled logistic regression, with negative (bone fracture) and positive (diabetes-related death) control outcomes. Results Of 52,341 eligible people, 19,599 (37.4%) started metformin. For COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, the maximally adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of metformin versus no antidiabetic was 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.35; 2-year risk difference 0.36%, 95% CI 0.09-0.62; intention-to-treat). The per-protocol HR for COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96-1.29). The Long COVID estimate was imprecise (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83-2.33; intention-to-treat). For bone fracture (negative control) the estimate was null (HR 1.00), but for diabetes-related deaths (positive control) it was elevated (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09-1.81), indicating unmeasured confounding. Conclusions The risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding. These findings align more closely with randomised evidence than earlier prevalent-user studies and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for COVID-19 prevention in newly diagnosed T2D. What is already known on this topic Observational studies and their meta-analyses have consistently reported 30-40% lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, yet most used prevalent-user designs that compare long-term survivors with mixed control groups and can overstate benefit. Randomised trials suggest little or no effect on mortality. What this study adds Using a new-user design in more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding rather than harm. How this study might affect research, practice or policy These findings align with randomised evidence and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for preventing severe or Long COVID in people with T2D. They also illustrate how new-user designs can reconcile discrepant observational and trial results and should be prioritised in future drug-repurposing studies. Lay summary Metformin is a medication commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, some studies suggested it might also protect against severe COVID-19, but many such studies had design limitations that could have made metformin look more beneficial than it truly is. In this study, we used NHS health records from over 52,000 adults in England who were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes to examine whether starting metformin shortly after diagnosis reduced the risk of being hospitalised or dying from COVID-19, being diagnosed with COVID-19. We found no evidence that starting metformin protected against any of these outcomes, although the effect on long COVID was imprecisely estimated. Our findings are consistent with results from clinical trials and suggest that metformin should not be expected to prevent severe COVID-19 in people with type 2 diabetes.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Cardiovascular risk factors have changed in the United States, but trends in prevalence, management, and predicted risk through the post-pandemic period remain incompletely characterized. Methods We analyzed 11 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) periods (1999–2000 through 2021–2023) among 60,199 nonpregnant adults aged ≥20 years. Survey-weighted regression assessed age-standardized trends, subgroup differences, and measurement-change sensitivity. We assessed awareness, treatment, and control of hypertension, dyslipidemia, and diabetes. PREVENT equations estimated 10- and 30-year risks among adults without self-reported cardiovascular disease (CVD). Results Obesity increased from 47.4% to 57.2% (odds ratio [OR] per decade, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.16–1.30), with class III obesity more than doubling (4.7% to 9.7%). Diabetes increased from 8.2% to 12.7% (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.19–1.34), while current smoking declined from 24.4% to 14.9% (OR, 0.76; 95% CI, 0.71–0.81). Hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic kidney disease, and prior CVD showed no significant linear trends, although mean systolic blood pressure (BP) (124.2 to 120.2 mm Hg) and total cholesterol (203.6 to 188.1 mg/dL) declined, alongside improvements in other lipids. Hypertension and dyslipidemia awareness and treatment increased, but BP control peaked at 32.5% in 2013–2014 before declining to 21.5%, while LDL cholesterol control rose from 17.0% to 34.2%. Diabetes awareness increased, but treatment trends were nonsignificant. Glycemic control peaked at 51.2% in 2003–2004 before declining to 41.9% (P for nonlinearity <0.001). Predicted 10-year total CVD risk declined from 5.66% to 5.28%; atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD) risk declined by 0.16 percentage points per decade (95% CI, −0.22 to −0.09), while heart failure (HF) risk increased by 0.10 (95% CI, 0.03–0.17). Their 2021–2023 estimates were nearly identical (3.20% and 3.19%, respectively); 30-year risks showed similar divergence. Conclusions Improvements in smoking, blood pressure, and lipids coexisted with rising obesity and diabetes, declining blood pressure control after earlier gains, and divergent predicted ASCVD and HF risks.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

research.abstract: Abstract Fruit flavor and aroma are determined by the sugars-to-acid ratio and, most importantly, by the specific profile and abundance of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). While over 550 VOCs have been identified in strawberry fruit, fewer than 20 are believed to be key for aroma, with esters representing the predominant class. A major and stable quantitative trait locus (QTL) explaining up to 40% of the phenotypic variation in several medium-chain esters (MCE) was mapped at about 19 Mb in chromosome 6A, through both QTL mapping in a biparental population and a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in a diverse collection. Integration of transcriptomic analyses from bulks contrasting in MCE content and multiple tissues of ‘Camarosa’ identified the cinnamoyl-CoA reductase gene FaCCR1(6A) as the most likely candidate underlying this QTL. Subcellular localization experiments indicated that FaCCR1(6A) is localized at the cytosol, and its transient overexpression in fruits significantly increased MCE content, confirming its pivotal role shaping fruit aroma. Although CCR enzymes are known for their involvement in the biosynthesis of monolignols, molecular docking analyses supported the interaction of FaCCR1(6A) with aliphatic acyl-CoA substrates . In vitro enzymatic assays further demonstrated that FaCCR1(6A) can catalyze the conversion of aliphatic acyl-CoA substrates to the corresponding medium-chain aldehydes. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized function of FaCCR1(6A) in volatile biosynthesis while providing a mechanistic explanation for the phenotypic differences associated with differential FaCCR1(6A) expression. Furthermore, we have developed a predictive KASP assay to facilitate the selection of superior cultivars with enhanced fruit aroma in strawberry breeding programs.

items.title: BEAGLE 4.1: A high-performance library for computation on phylogenetic trees across diverse parallel architectures
items.summary: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

items.summary: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. research.abstract: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human-cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. It shows benefits for gene discovery and gene prioritization and in our application expands available functional follow-up data, allowing us to leverage cattle eQTL data to resolve human GWAS loci. The method and underlying philosophy presented here are transferable to other shared phenotypes across several species.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 18 loci (L = 26,700 aligned columns; Lagomorpha outgroups, Sciuromorpha, Castorimorpha, Dipodoidea, invasive Muridae, and New World Cricetidae: Arvicolinae, Neotominae, and Sigmodontinae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three North American PopSets (Peromyscus maniculatus, Sigmodon hispidus, and Urocitellus parryii; 3 × N = 36 = 108 conspecific isolates) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The continental radiation of rodents (Order Rodentia) across North America via Paleogene Beringian corridors, Miocene grassland expansions, and Great American Biotic Interchange exchanges—coupled with the Anthropocene introduction of Old World commensal murids—established both the foundational small-mammal trophic guilds of Nearctic ecosystems and the primary sylvatic reservoirs for North America's major rodent-borne zoonoses. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across an 18-locus, 64-species Glires supermatrix (L = 26,700 aligned columns with 7,979 parsimony-informative sites and 8,803 distinct site patterns) paired with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three conspecific North American population datasets (3 × N = 36 = 108 isolates) benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors the Glires root (Lagomorpha vs. Rodentia) at 65.2 Ma, Crown Rodentia at 56.8 Ma, the Sciuromorpha–Castorimorpha split at 36.4 Ma, Myodonta (Dipodoidea vs. Muroidea) at 46.5 Ma, the Muridae–Cricetidae divergence at 24.8 Ma, Crown Cricetidae at 18.6 Ma, and the New World Neotominae–Sigmodontinae split at 13.4 Ma. Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on the Sin Nombre hantavirus endothelial receptor ITGB3 beta-3 integrin (omega = 0.5319), intermediate selective constraint on the high-altitude and fossorial hypoxia axis EPAS1/HBB (omega = 0.0343) and rodenticide-detoxification locus VKORC1/CYP2C (omega = 0.2572), and diversifying positive selection on bacterial pattern-recognition receptors TLR2/TLR4 (omega = 0.2631) and the New World Arenavirus receptor TFRC transferrin receptor 1 apical domain (omega = 0.1453). Across the three single-species PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve post-glacial forest/oak-mast expansion and contemporary ENSO Sin Nombre hantavirus / Lyme disease amplification in the North American deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus, N = 36, Ne = 433,194 to 653,847; *BEAST = 667,970), northward agricultural grassland expansion and Black Creek Canal / Tamiami viral irruptions in the hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus, N = 36, Ne = 1,534,254 to 1,753,302; *BEAST = 1,808,005), and post-LGM Beringian steppe-tundra recolonization and high-latitude permafrost-thaw dynamics in the Arctic ground squirrel (Urocitellus parryii, N = 36, Ne = 707,606 to 1,687,680; *BEAST = 1,740,336), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 42.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.88 s vs. 595.24 s Hybrid and 1861.52 s full External UFBoot). items.title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
items.summary: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an…

research.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

items.title: Whole-genome analysis of drug resistance and transmission patterns in Mycobacterium tuberculosis from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan.
items.summary: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A…

research.abstract: UNLABELLED: The emergence of drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains presents a significant challenge to tuberculosis (TB) control programmes worldwide, particularly in high-burden countries, such as Pakistan. This study characterises the genomic diversity and drug resistance mutation profiles of M. tuberculosis isolates from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa using whole-genome sequencing (WGS). A total of 35 clinical M. tuberculosis isolates underwent WGS. Sequence data were quality-filtered and mapped to the H37Rv reference genome, characterising variants, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Lineage classification, drug resistance profiling, and identification of resistance mutations were performed using TB-Profiler software. SNP-based clustering was used to infer recent transmission events. All four major M. tuberculosis lineages (L1-L4) were detected; however, more than half of the isolates belonged to lineage L3 (CAS, n = 19; 54.3%). Almost all isolates were drug-resistant (34/35), including pre-extensively drug-resistant (pre-XDR, n = 15; 42.9%) and multidrug-resistant (MDR, n = 14; 40.0%) strains. The most frequent resistance-associated mutations included katG S315T (27/35) and inhA c.-777C > T (4/35) for isoniazid resistance, rpoB S450L (24/35) for rifampicin resistance, embB M306I/V (18/35) for ethambutol resistance, and gyrA D94G (8/35) and A90V (5/35) for fluoroquinolone resistance. Compensatory mutations were observed in rpoC and ahpC. Mutations associated with bedaquiline and clofazimine resistance (mmpR5 c.140dupA, c.138_139dupTG) were detected in single isolates. Interestingly, one isolate exhibited a deletion encompassing mmpR5, mmpL5, and mmpS5, potentially increasing bedaquiline susceptibility. Phylogenetic analysis using 6,635 genome-wide SNPs identified two transmission clusters with < 9 SNPs differences, suggesting ongoing local transmission. These results highlight the presence of drug-resistant M. tuberculosis strains in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, encompassing both globally recognised and novel resistance-associated mutations. Our findings underscore the critical need to integrate WGS into TB surveillance and control programmes in Pakistan to guide targeted interventions and curb the spread of resistant strains. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62482-7.

items.title: A timeline for evolution of metabolism in early microbes
items.summary: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4…

research.abstract: The metabolism of early microbes shaped our planet's chemistry and enabled more life to evolve. However, it remains uncertain when many forms of metabolism arose and which organisms carried them out. Here we combine machine learning, metabolic networks, and phylogenomics of microbes to date 14 forms of metabolism and 6 other traits. We find that metabolism evolved in three waves, starting >3.4 billion years ago (Ga) with fermentation and sulfur compound respiration. A second wave began ~3.2 Ga with aerobic respiration and growth, while a third began ~1.4 Ga with further specialization. We compared these predictions with independent dates from the geochemical record, and agreement with conservative dates was good (CCC = 0.81 to 0.89). Several forms of metabolism are invisible in the geochemical record, and our approach dates these forms, too. Our results reconcile different lines of evidence for microbial evolution and provide a fuller picture of early Earth.

Design: A retrospective, cross-sectional study. Participants: Individuals with diabetes who responded to the Medicare Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), a nationally representative survey of U.S. households (2013-2022). Methods…

research.abstract: Purpose: To determine whether English proficiency is associated with diabetic retinopathy screening rates among patients with diabetes in the United States. Design: A retrospective, cross-sectional study. Participants: Individuals with diabetes who responded to the Medicare Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), a nationally representative survey of U.S. households (2013-2022). Methods: Survey-weighted, multivariable logistic regression. Main Outcome Measures: Adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 1) having ever received a dilated fundus examination (DFE) and 2) having received consecutive year DFEs. Results: The analytic sample included 11,441 respondents representing a weighted sample of 15,107,166 U.S. civilians with diabetes per year from 2013-2022. The mean age was 62 years (SD: 14 years), and 50% were female. Individuals with limited English proficiency (LEP) comprised 11.6% of the cohort. Respondents with LEP had lower odds of ever having received a DFE compared to English-proficient respondents (aOR=0.729, 95% CI: 0.541-0.976). The association between having consecutive year DFEs and English proficiency was non-significant (aOR=1.189, 95% CI: 0.917-1.541). In sensitivity analyses using a definition of LEP as speaking English less than well, LEP was associated with lower odds of ever having a DFE (aOR=0.632, 95% CI: 0.460-0.869) and higher odds of consecutive year exams (aOR=1.415, 95% CI: 1.057-1.896). Conclusions: LEP status was associated with lower odds of ever having had a DFE and equal or greater odds of having consecutive year DFEs. Efforts to reduce language-related disparities for patients with LEP should focus on improving initial access to ophthalmologic care.

items.title: Routine Xpert MTB/XDR for Tuberculosis Drug-Resistance Surveillance in Northern Morocco: A Four-Year Programmatic Analysis
items.summary: Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring. We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco…

research.abstract: Abstract Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring. We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco. We retrospectively analyzed 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes performed from April 2022 to July 2026 and linked available Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra results with target-level molecular outputs. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was detected in 203 episodes (78.7%), of which 188 (92.6%) had an interpretable rifampicin result. Molecular rifampicin resistance was detected in 75/188 episodes (39.9%) and isoniazid resistance in 71/192 (37.0%); molecular multidrug-resistant tuberculosis was identified in 51/184 (27.7%) episodes with paired results. Among 186 episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 21/112 (18.8%) rifampicin-susceptible and 54/74 (73.0%) rifampicin-resistant episodes. Among 92 resistant episodes with complete profiles, 66 (71.7%) showed resistance to two or more drug classes. rpoB3- and rpoB4- associated signals predominated among rifampicin-resistant episodes, katG -associated signals among isoniazid-resistant episodes, and gyrA targets among fluoroquinolone-resistant episodes. Mixed wild-type and mutation-associated signals occurred across rpoB and gyrA . These findings support the use of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing as a component of regional drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance, enabling systematic characterization of multiclass resistance and molecular resistance patterns within routine diagnostic networks. Such molecular surveillance should be integrated with phenotypic susceptibility testing and genomic sequencing to resolve discordant, atypical, or clinically consequential profiles and build a more comprehensive regional resistance-monitoring system.

items.title: R-pyocin-mediated selection restores aminoglycoside sensitivity in a pan-drug resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolate
items.summary: The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged…

research.abstract: Abstract The global escalation of antibiotic resistance is a critical threat necessitating innovative strategies to provide new therapeutic options and restore the efficacy of conventional drugs. Pseudomonas aeruginosa exemplifies this challenge by utilizing a robust genomic resistome to persist in clinical settings. Here, we demonstrate that R-pyocins (phage-like bactericidal particles) can be leveraged not as conventional biocides but as precise selective forces to drive an evolutionary trap. We subjected the laboratory strains PAO1 and PAK and the clinical pan-drug-resistant (PDR) wound isolate MRSN 6220 to R-pyocin selective pressure. Under sustained R-pyocin pressure, every pyomelanogenic variant we recovered evaded R-pyocin killing through large-scale chromosomal deletions spanning 250-388 kbp. These deletions encompass a conserved region harboring the galU gene (essential for LPS synthesis), the hmgA gene (yielding a pyomelanogenic ‘brown’ phenotype), and the mexXYZ multidrug efflux operon. While the loss of galU confers broad cross-resistance to R-pyocins by likely truncating the LPS receptor, the concurrent excision of mexXY induces profound collateral sensitivity to aminoglycosides. These deletions also eliminate critical virulence factors and biofilm clusters, including the hcnABC , exoY , phzABCDEFG , and cup operons. In a Galleria mellonella model, the resulting brown mutants were non-lethal, and in infected murine wound tissue treated ex vivo with gentamicin they exhibited a significant 3-log reduction in bacterial load, whereas the pan-drug-resistant ancestor did not. This work establishes a framework for utilizing R-pyocins as evolutionary steering agents that couple the acquisition of R-pyocin resistance to the reversion of multidrug resistance into an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state. Importance Pan-drug-resistant (PDR) pathogens demand novel strategies that both kill and restore antibiotic efficacy. Here, we describe an evolutionary trap for Pseudomonas aeruginosa , where selection for R-pyocin resistance drives large-scale (∼300 kb) chromosomal remodeling. Although these deletions confer R-pyocin immunity via loss of the galU gene, they simultaneously collapse the pathogen’s virulence and defense. Crucially, the excision of the mexXY efflux operon resensitizes a PDR clinical isolate to conventional aminoglycosides, while the collateral loss of critical virulence and biofilm clusters abrogates pathogenesis. By coupling resistance acquisition to substantial fitness costs, our work establishes a framework for using R-pyocins to force predictable evolutionary trade-offs, driving the reversion of multidrug resistance to an attenuated, biofilm-deficient, and clinically manageable state.

items.title: Primary Pre-Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (Pre XDR-TB) Pulmonary Tuberculosis with Diabetes Mellitus: A Case Report
items.summary: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge in tuberculosis control, and the occurrence of resistance in patients without any prior treatment history raises concern about the transmission of resistant strains within the community.We report the case of a 63-year-old woman presenting with cough for more than two months, marked weight loss, and intermittent fever, without any previous…

research.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis remains a major challenge in tuberculosis control, and the occurrence of resistance in patients without any prior treatment history raises concern about the transmission of resistant strains within the community.We report the case of a 63-year-old woman presenting with cough for more than two months, marked weight loss, and intermittent fever, without any previous tuberculosis treatment or known contact with a tuberculosis patient.She had a history of diabetes mellitus.Physical examination revealed bronchial breath sounds with rhonchi, and chest radiography revealed infiltration at the right upper lung apex.Rapid molecular testing detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with resistance to rifampicin, and second-line drug susceptibility testing further revealed additional resistance to isoniazid, fluoroquinolone, and ethionamide, leading to a diagnosis of primary pre-extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis.Random blood glucose was elevated and was managed with insulin, while mild hypochromic anaemia was managed with iron supplementation.The patient received bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, and remained clinically stable without significant adverse effects after one week of therapy.This case highlights the importance of vigilance for primary drug-resistant tuberculosis and the role of rapid molecular testing in early diagnosis and appropriate treatment selection.
