research.abstract: Abstract Codon-based maximum likelihood models are the workhorse of molecular selection analysis, yet standard workflows assume that the input sequence alignment and phylogenetic tree are known without error. In practice, heuristic aligners ignore the genetic code and phylogeny, which packs non-homologous codons into shared columns across insertion-deletion loops and inflates gene-wide false-positive rates above 80%. This sequential division of labor is statistically suboptimal and computationally wasteful. Here, we present WALRUS ( W heatstone A lignment and L ikelihood R ate U nification for S election), a unified engine in H y P hy 3 ( https://github.com/veg/hyphy-3 ) that maps unaligned coding sequences to a coordinate-consistent selection atlas in one run. From a single Inside–Outside likelihood table, the pipeline repairs reading frames, co-estimates a codon alignment and Ohmic reticulate network, models directional base-composition drift, and evaluates eight selection tests (BUSTED-E, aBSREL, RELAX, FEL, dFEL, MEME, Contrast-FEL, and PRIME). Across 10,020 simulated alignments, WALRUS recovers 94.6% of true columns on the 800 INDELible replicates and cuts indel-driven false positives from 44.7%– 58.1% to 4.4% under BUSTED (21.1%– 21.4% to 1.4% under BUSTED-E). Under Zipfian indel saturation, false positives drop four-fold (33.3%– 83.3% to 17.0%– 20.5%), while 11, 190 avian orthogroup runs execute 6.6–35.8-fold faster and cut housekeeping false positives 13-fold (28-fold on ultraconserved genes) proteome-wide.

items.title: Decoding positive selection in Mycobacterium tuberculosis with phylogeny-guided graph attention models.
items.summary: MOTIVATION: Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a…

research.abstract: Abstract Motivation Positive selection is a key evolutionary force in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , driving the emergence of adaptive mutations that influence drug resistance, transmissibility, and virulence of tuberculosis. Phylogenetic trees capture the hierarchical evolutionary relationships among isolates, making them an ideal framework for detecting such adaptive signals. Here, we present a phylogeny-guided graph attention network approach, coupled with a novel method for converting SNP-annotated phylogenetic trees into graph structures suitable for graph neural network processing. Results Using a dataset of 1000 M. tuberculosis isolates, representing the four main lineages, and 206 single-nucleotide variants (75 resistance-associated and 131 neutral) spanning 79 drug-resistance genes, we constructed graphs where nodes represented individual isolates and edges reflected phylogenetic distances. To reduce noise and highlight local evolutionary structure, we pruned edges between isolates separated by more than seven internal nodes. Node features were encoded as binary indicators of SNP presence or absence, and the graph attention network (GAT) architecture comprised two attention layers with a residual connection, followed by global attention pooling and a multilayer perceptron classifier. The model achieved higher accuracy (0.81, AUC 0.82) than a homoplasy-count baseline (0.71) on the held-out test set. Under repeated cross-validation, however, F1 scores did not differ significantly (0.56 vs. 0.58; paired Wilcoxon p = 0.98), reflecting a specificity-sensitivity trade-off: the GAT favoured specificity (0.89), the baseline favoured sensitivity. Applying the model to 138 WHO-classified “uncertain” variants identified 28 high-confidence candidates, including rpoC Ile491Val (rifampicin, compensatory), ubiA Arg240Cys (ethambutol), and rpsA Ala412Val (pyrazinamide). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of encoding phylogenetic trees as graph neural network-compatible structures and the utility of attention-based models for detecting positive-selection signals, supporting genomic surveillance and prioritisation of candidates for experimental validation. Availability and Implementation The source code for the model can be found at https://github.com/linfeng-wang/Phylogeny-Guided_GAT .

items.title: Direct Sputum Sequencing Reveals Mycobacterium tuberculosis Diversity Underrepresented by Culture in a High TB-Burden Setting

Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods: We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from…

research.abstract: Background: Whole-genome sequencing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) commonly relies on culture-derived isolates, potentially altering the bacterial populations represented. Direct sputum whole-genome sequencing (dsWGS) may better capture lineage composition and within-host variant diversity. Methods: We compared targeted-enrichment dsWGS with WGS of matched culture-derived isolates from participants initiating treatment for rifampicin-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis in Worcester, South Africa. We assessed sequencing performance, technical reproducibility, sputum-sampling variability, lineage and variant concordance, and resistance-associated variation, and explored associations with baseline clinical characteristics and treatment response. Results: Of 218 clinical dsWGS reactions, 139 passed sequencing quality criteria, yielding 113 eligible baseline sputum-culture pairs. Mixed-lineage infection was detected in 72/113 (63.7%) sputum specimens versus 7/113 (6.2%) matched cultures; 66/113 (58.4%) pairs showed reduced lineage diversity following culture. Permutation analysis indicated preferential retention of Lineage 2 and depletion of Lineage 3 after culture. Technical replicates preserved dominant phylotype assignments (median SNP Jaccard similarity 0.863), while independently collected sputum specimens showed greater variability. Among 38 concordant single-lineage pairs, 35,540/38,311 (92.8%) pair-specific variant observations were shared after filtering and raw-read recovery, while 2,497 (6.5%) were sputum-unique and 274 (0.7%) culture-unique. Discordance was concentrated among variable variants; 88.0% of shared variants variable in at least one specimen had higher allele frequencies in culture. No sputum-unique WHO Grade 1 or 2 resistance-associated mutations were identified in the strain-controlled subset, whereas eight mixed-lineage sputum samples versus three matched cultures harboured such mutations. Higher baseline low-frequency variant burden showed non-significant trends towards delayed culture conversion (log-rank p=0.144) and unfavourable treatment outcomes (log-rank p=0.400). Conclusions: Direct-sputum WGS revealed M. tuberculosis lineage and low-frequency variant diversity that was not fully represented by matched culture-derived genomes, despite high overall genomic concordance. These findings highlight the complementary value of direct-sputum sequencing for characterising within-host diversity, while suggesting that the representation of bacterial populations following culture may vary across epidemiological settings. Further research is needed to improve the accuracy of minority-variant detection and establish the clinical relevance of diversity measured directly from sputum.

items.title: HLA-Resolve: Four-field HLA typing and MHC variant detection from long-read hybrid capture
items.summary: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. research.abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. Long-read sequencing is increasingly used in HLA typing because of its ability to phase variants across long distances, but many long-read HLA typing workflows still rely on long-range PCR. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow for MHC genotyping that pairs hybrid capture with long-read sequencing on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore, using single-step enzymatic fragmentation and barcoding to enable automated library preparation. The hybrid capture panel enriches both classical and non-classical HLA Class I and Class II genes, as well as all 69 protein-coding MHC Class III genes. We introduce HLA-Resolve, a bioinformatic tool that types HLA genes from PacBio reads via phased full-gene sequence reconstruction, and we benchmark the capture assay and HLA-Resolve together across 32 geographically diverse samples. With PacBio data, variant calling achieved F1 scores of 99.8% for SNVs and 98.4% for indels against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. HLA-Resolve showed 99.5% allele concordance with reference typings from the International Histocompatibility Working Group and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) at three-field resolution and 90.5% at four-field resolution, outperforming three other open-source long-read HLA typers on our HiFi hybrid capture reads. The full-gene sequences reconstructed by HLA-Resolve showed zero edit distance to the corresponding HPRC assemblies in 95% of comparisons. HLA-Resolve also showed high accuracy with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, achieving 99.4% two-field concordance across 146 public PacBio WGS libraries and 99.5% three-field concordance across the 52 with full-resolution reference typings. Although developed for the MHC, the workflow is customizable to any gene set, providing a general framework for high-resolution genotyping.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 16 loci (L = 23,924 aligned columns; African Catarrhini and Neotropical Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three independent PopSets (Alouatta spp., Sapajus/Cebus, and Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The colonization of South America by African anthropoid primates during the Middle to Late Eocene and their subsequent diversification across Neotropical forest strata into five ecologically specialized families (Pitheciidae, Atelidae, Cebidae, Callitrichidae, and Aotidae) represent one of mammalogy's classic trans-oceanic adaptive radiations. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across a 16-locus, 64-species primate supermatrix (L = 23,924 aligned columns with 10,254 parsimony-informative sites and 11,093 distinct site patterns) coupled with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three localized Neotropical population datasets benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors Crown Primates at 74.0 Ma, the trans-Atlantic Simiiformes split between African Catarrhini (crown 28.5 Ma) and Neotropical Platyrrhini at 43.2 Ma (stem rafting window 43.2–24.2 Ma across the Eocene Atlantic), and Crown Platyrrhini at 24.2 Ma, followed by crown radiations of Pitheciidae (19.8 Ma), Atelidae (16.8 Ma), Cebidae (19.5 Ma), Callitrichidae (14.8 Ma), and Aotidae (11.4 Ma). Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on Pro8-oxytocin OXT/OXTR neuroendocrine signaling (omega = 0.4905), intermediate selective constraint on TAS2R bitter-taste receptors (omega = 0.7442) and ENAM/GHR dental and phyletic-dwarfism loci (omega = 0.8436), and diversifying and balancing selection on duplicated RNASE1/CHIA folivory-insectivory digestive enzymes (omega = 1.2118) and X-linked OPN1LW spectral-tuning opsin exons (omega = 2.4891). Across the three localized PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve late Quaternary trans-Andean expansion and contemporary yellow fever epizootic pressure in howler monkeys (Alouatta, Ne = 628,056 to 977,186; *BEAST = 1,007,674), Pleistocene Cerrado/Caatinga dry-corridor colonization and stone-tool nut-cracking persistence in capuchins (Sapajus/Cebus, Ne = 1,042,598 to 1,376,278; *BEAST = 1,411,397), and Atlantic Forest fragmentation followed by metapopulation translocation recovery in callitrichid marmosets and tamarins (Callithrix/Saguinus/Leontopithecus, Ne = 469,859 to 912,085; *BEAST = 940,542), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 29.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.54 s vs. 404.82 s Hybrid and 3127.88 s full External UFBoot). research.abstract: Abstract Background The HSP70 family maintains cellular proteostasis and mediates vertebrate responses to environmental stress. The Chinese alligator ( Alligator sinensis ), an ectothermic crocodilian, undergoes winter dormancy characterized by cessation of feeding, reduced activity, and metabolic depression. However, the evolutionary patterns of the HSP70 family across vertebrates and their potential relevance to winter dormancy in crocodilians remain poorly understood. We characterized the HSP70 family across 24 vertebrate species, focusing on the molecular evolution of HSPA12A along crocodilian lineages and its seasonal expression in the hypothalamus of the Chinese alligator. Results Using HMMER- and BLAST-based searches, we identified 355 HSP70 family members, with 11–28 members per species. Phylogenetic, synteny, and subcellular localization analyses indicated that the family is broadly conserved but exhibits subfamily- and lineage-associated divergence. Under two foreground schemes in which the terminal branches of two winter-dormant crocodilians or all four crocodilian species were jointly designated as foreground, HSPA12A showed an elevated relative evolutionary rate and significant evidence of positive selection. HyPhy aBSREL supported episodic diversifying selection on the A. sinensis HSPA12A terminal branch. Public RNA-seq data showed that HSPA12A expression was highest in the hypothalamus among sampled female tissues and was higher in winter than in summer (600.0 and 329.2 TPM, respectively). Western blotting and immunofluorescence analyses showed descriptive differences between the examined specimens, with higher HSPA12A protein abundance and a higher density of cells double-positive for anti-HSPA12A antibody immunoreactivity and NeuN in winter. Because each RNA-seq, western blotting, and immunofluorescence comparison included only one biological specimen per season, these observations were treated as descriptive, and no inferential statistical comparisons were performed. Conclusions The vertebrate HSP70 family is broadly conserved but shows differentiation among subfamilies and lineages. The evolutionary analyses indicate a broader crocodilian-lineage-associated pattern of HSPA12A evolution that cannot be attributed specifically to winter dormancy. Separately, the descriptive transcriptomic and preliminary protein-level observations provide a basis for considering HSPA12A as a candidate for further investigation in relation to winter physiology in the Chinese alligator. These findings do not establish winter dormancy as the selective driver of HSPA12A evolution, and its biological function and causal role remain to be determined.

authors.affiliation: Department of Clinical Sciences, Faculty of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, University of Layyah, Layyah, 31200, Pakistan

research.abstract: Camelids have evolved remarkable physiological adaptations enabling survival in extreme desert environments, yet the genomic basis of these traits remains incompletely understood. We conducted a comparative genomic analysis across eleven mammalian species, including three Old World camels, four New World camels, two additional artiodactyls (pig, cattle), and two outgroups (human, mouse), to identify lineage-specific molecular signatures of adaptation. Using OrthoFinder, we constructed orthologous gene families and identified 11,861 single-copy orthologs across all species. We detected significant copy-number changes in cytochrome P450 gene families, with expansion of CYP2J and contraction of CYP4F in the camelid ancestor, suggesting a shift toward anti-inflammatory eicosanoid signaling. Branch-site analyses identified 47 high-confidence positively selected genes in Old World camels, including HACD3, a fatty acid elongation enzyme harboring an ultraconserved substitution (D270N). Structural modeling and conservation analysis suggest that this substitution may hypothetically alter protein conformation, but this prediction awaits experimental validation. Tissue-specific RNA-seq analysis confirmed that HACD3 is expressed in camel kidney and liver, tissues central to lipid metabolism and water conservation. Systematic screening for inactivating mutations identified ten high-confidence pseudogenized genes, including CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, enriched in lipid metabolism and epidermal pathways. The adaptive significance of these losses is currently hypothetical and inferred from homologous gene studies in mice and humans; because some of the cited genes are paralogs rather than orthologs, and because mouse and human phenotypes may not transfer to camels, these inferences are hypothesis-generating only and do not establish camel gene function. Experimental validation confirmed pseudogenization of TAS2R16, and cell-based calcium-signalling assays showed that the camel receptor fails to respond to salicin. This establishes loss of receptor function but not its adaptive significance; both dietary-breadth and neutral (relaxed-selection or drift) explanations remain compatible with the data. For CES3, CPA3, and PLA2G2F, functional consequences in camels remain unverified and require camel-specific experimental validation. Collectively, these results provide a comprehensive framework of gene family evolution, positive selection, and gene loss underlying desert adaptation in camelids, while highlighting that expression patterns are correlative only and do not demonstrate that the identified variants alter protein function or physiology.

research.abstract: Adaptive evolution frequently proceeds through the co-option of pre-existing biological functions, yet the molecular mechanisms by which such co-option generates new adaptive traits over contemporary evolutionary timescales remain poorly understood. Herbicide-resistant weeds provide a powerful model for addressing this question because enhanced herbicide metabolism has repeatedly evolved within only a few decades. Here, we show that resistance to cyhalofop-butyl in Echinochloa crus-galli evolved through the co-option of EcNIT4A2 , which encodes a nitrilase that normally functions in ethylene-associated cyanide detoxification. Genetic mapping, transcriptomics and transgenic analyses identified EcNIT4A2 as the major determinant of resistance. A D317G substitution enhanced its herbicide-detoxifying activity. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that this substitution facilitates substrate access to the catalytic pocket. A promoter structural variant markedly increased EcNIT4A2 expression. Our findings reveal how coding and regulatory changes can jointly drive the co-option and optimization of a conserved metabolic function during rapid adaptation under intense anthropogenic selection.

research.abstract: Abstract Thienothiazolocarboxamides (TTCs) were discovered as a hit in a whole cell screen for new antituberculosis agents. These molecules were rapidly cidal under both replicating and non-replicating conditions and killed Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) in macrophages. The heterobicyclic core of this scaffold was essential for activity and resistance to these agents was mediated by loss of EthA, a flavin containing monooxygenase also responsible for the bioactivation of ethionamide. EthA-mediated activation of TTCs in whole cells was found to produce mycothiol adducts and RNAseq profiles revealed a mechanism of action identical to the fungal mycotoxins patulin and nidulalin A. EthA oxidizes the sulfur of the thiazole ring to create a relatively stable sulfenic acid that reacts with cellular thiols. This unique, replication-independent, mechanism suggests the possibility that these molecules may contribute significantly to shortening the duration of tuberculosis chemotherapy.

items.title: HERACLES for fast and accurate likelihood-based reconstruction of massive lineages
items.summary: CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas distance-based…

research.abstract: Abstract CRISPR-based lineage recording technologies can trace the ancestry of hundreds of thousands of cells, yet reconstructing accurate phylogenies at this scale remains computationally challenging. Likelihood-based methods employ explicit evolutionary models of CRISPR editing that improve tree accuracy but require computationally expensive searches over tree topologies, whereas greedy distance-based alternatives scale efficiently but their accuracy requires distances that faithfully represent the true phylogeny. Here, we introduce HERACLES, which optimizes cell coordinates in hyperbolic space under a quartet-based composite likelihood of CRISPR editing. By recovering local branching structures directly from embedded distances, HERACLES guides continuous optimization with an explicit evolutionary model without repeatedly constructing and evaluating complete phylogenies. Across simulated benchmarks, HERACLES improves reconstruction accuracy over existing methods and scales to lineages containing 150,000 cells in about four hours on a single GPU. On experimental KP-tracer and PEtracer datasets, HERACLES reconstructs phylogenies consistent with independent anatomical annotations and temporal lineage markers. Its flexible likelihood framework also accommodates different recording mechanisms, and incorporating sequential editing improves reconstruction of simulated DNA Typewriter lineages. Together, these results establish continuous optimization of local evolutionary relationships as a scalable and flexible approach to probabilistic lineage reconstruction. Code availability HERACLES is available at https://github.com/morrislab/HERACLES .

items.title: Optimizing dosing strategies for children with leprosy: A weight-banded dosing approach
items.summary: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better…

research.abstract: BackgroundDosing guidance for children with leprosy remains operationally challenging. For children under 10 years of age, current WHO recommendations rely on mg/kg dosing of the three separate components of leprosy multidrug therapy, which are difficult to implement in routine care and may result in inconsistent drug exposures. Weight-banded dosing offers a pragmatic alternative that better aligns with pharmacokinetic principles and existing drug formulations. MethodologyA pharmacokinetic simulation study was conducted to develop harmonized weight-banded dosing regimens for rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone in children aged 2 to <10 years. Using the WHO dosing tool, drug exposures across harmonized weight bands were simulated and adult-equivalent systemic exposure (80- 125% of adult area under the concentration-time curve) targeted. Predicted exposures were contextualized against safety reference regimens used in tuberculosis meningitis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, and leprosy. An iterative review process involving the WHO Technical Working Group on leprosy in children ensured clinical and operational feasibility. ResultsProposed weight-banded multidrug therapy regimens achieved adult-equivalent exposures across most weight bands. Predicted exposures modestly exceeded 125% of adult levels at the lower end of selected weight bands but remained well below safety benchmarks, namely exposures associated with daily rifampicin therapy for tuberculosis meningitis and clofazimine regimens for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. Dapsone exposures were comparable to those achieved with current leprosy dosing. The existing 10-14-year-old child MDT blister pack could be used without modification in children weighing 25-39.9 kg and with limited tablet or gel capsule removal in children weighing 6-24.9 kg. ConclusionsA harmonized weight-banded dosing strategy was developed that enables effective, practical dosing of leprosy multidrug therapy in children under 10 years using existing free-of-charge blister packs provided through WHO. This approach improves dosing consistency, supports programmatic implementation, and provides a rational interim solution while child-friendly formulations are being developed. Author SummaryLeprosy continues to affect children in many low-resource settings, yet guidance on how to dose treatment in younger children remains limited. Current recommendations often require clinicians to calculate mg/kg doses, which can be difficult in practice and may not match the oral formulations that are available. In this study, we used computer-based simulations to develop a simplified dosing approach for the three drugs used to treat leprosy. We showed that grouping children into weight bands, rather than calculating individual doses, can achieve drug exposures similar to those seen in adults, where treatment is known to be effective. Importantly, we found that these doses can be delivered using existing pre-packed treatment kits by removing selected dose units, making this approach practical in routine care. This work provides a more straightforward and reliable way to treat children with leprosy, reducing the burden on clinicians and improving access to treatment. However, challenges remain, including the lack of child-friendly formulations and limited data on how these drugs behave in children. Further studies are needed to improve treatment for this vulnerable population.

items.title: Uncoupling mycomembrane biogenesis from mycolic acid synthesis reveals a distinct role for mycoloyltransferases in mycobacterial cell division.

A defining feature of the mycomembrane is its enrichment in mycolic acids, long-chain -branched, {beta}-hydroxylated…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Bacteria of the order Mycobacteriales, including the genera Mycobacterium and Corynebacterium , possess a unique outer membrane, termed the mycomembrane, which is structurally and chemically distinct from the lipopolysaccharide-containing outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. A defining feature of the mycomembrane is its enrichment in mycolic acids, long-chain α-branched, β-hydroxylated fatty acids that occur as trehalose monomycolate (TMM), trehalose dimycolate (TDM), or are esterified to arabinogalactan, an unusual polymer that is itself covalently linked to peptidoglycan (PG). Mycoloyltransferases are Mycobacteriales - specific enzymes described to catalyze the transfer of mycolic acids from trehalose monomycolate (TMM) to various cell envelope acceptors, including trehalose and arabinogalactan. In several species, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis , these proteins are essential for viability; however, their occurrence as multiple paralogs with partially redundant functions has hindered the precise assignment of their cellular roles. Previously, we showed that Corynebacterium glutamicum remains viable in the absence of mycolic acids, and thus without a mycomembrane, following deletion of pks , the gene required for mycolic acid biosynthesis. Building on this finding, we systematically deleted all genes encoding mycoloyltransferases in C. glutamicum to further disclose their collective function in the cell. The resulting Δ myts mutant lacked arabinogalactan-bound mycolates and TDM, and continued to synthesize TMM. While this major outer membrane glycolipid is highly abundant, the Δ myts strain failed to assemble a mycomembrane and displayed pronounced cell aggregation. Deletion of mycoloyltransferases also caused very severe defects in cell division and morphogenesis that are not observed in a Δ pks strain unable to synthesize mycolic acids. Together, these results demonstrate that mycoloyltransferases are essential for mycomembrane assembly but dispensable for TMM biosynthesis, and reveal an important role for these enzymes in cell division that is independent of their canonical mycolic acid transfer activity. SIGNIFICANCE How the mycomembrane is assembled and anchored to the cell wall remains a central question in Mycobacteriales, where this outer membrane is necessary for envelope integrity and intrinsic antibiotic resistance. By genetically separating mycolic acid synthesis from their incorporation into the outer membrane, we identify arabinogalactan-linked mycolates as the critical determinant for initiating membrane assembly. Importantly, we also uncover a role for mycoloyltransferases beyond their canonical function in lipid metabolism, revealing a functional link with cell division. These findings point to a critical role of Mycoloyltransferases in the coordination between outer membrane biogenesis and bacterial cytokinesis.

research.journal: Otago University Research Archive (University of Otago)
research.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infects the lungs and causes the disease tuberculosis, which the World Health Organization estimates causes 1 million deaths across the globe annually. Emergence of drug resistance has lessened the effectiveness and requires a longer duration of treatment. Bedaquiline was approved by the FDA in 2012 to treat multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis cases when no other treatment was viable. TBAJ-587, a derivative of Bedaquiline, has been found to be more effective at treating multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis, and has fewer adverse effects. The aim of this project was to test if strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis that have a mutation in Rv0678 causing overexpression of the MmpS5L5 efflux pump will evolve high-level resistance to TBAJ-587 at a higher frequency than wild-type strains. This was done by growing a wild-type M. tuberculosis strain and a ∆Rv0678 mutant on plates of 7H11 agar containing increasing concentrations of TBAJ-587, then selecting isolates and confirming resistance using an anti-microbial susceptibility assay to determine the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of the isolated strains. 72 strains from the wild-type background were assayed, and 114 from the ∆Rv0678 background were assayed. The resistant ∆Rv0678 strains tended to have higher minimum inhibitory concentrations that the resistant WT strains. Mutations in the WT strains were found throughout Rv0678, and D28, E6, A62 and I66 mutations in atpE, as well as L168 in atpB. Similar atpE mutations were found in ∆Rv0678, with the addition of mutations in A63 of atpE.

items.title: Network-level selection constrains the adaptive evolution of gene expression noise in regulatory genes in changing environments
items.summary: Gene expression levels vary from cell to cell, even between clonal cells in identical environmental conditions. This variance is termed "expression noise" and is partially genetically encoded and subject to selection. While gene expression noise is detrimental in constant environments where the expression level is under stabilizing selection, it can be beneficial in changing environments, when…

research.abstract: Abstract Gene expression levels vary from cell to cell, even between clonal cells in identical environmental conditions. This variance is termed “expression noise” and is partially genetically encoded and subject to selection. While gene expression noise is detrimental in constant environments where the expression level is under stabilizing selection, it can be beneficial in changing environments, when the phenotype is far from the optimum. However, expression noise propagates along the gene regulatory network, making the evolution of connected genes interdependent. Here, we explore how the position of the gene in the gene network constrains the evolution of its expression noise and expression mean under selection using in silico evolution experiments. We simulate the evolution of populations of model gene regulatory networks under directional and fluctuating selection on the gene expression level while allowing the basal expression level and expression noise level to mutate. We find that expression noise is only transiently favoured under directional selection, indicating a co-evolutionary dynamic between expression mean and noise during adaptation. On the other hand, high levels of noise are persistently maintained under fluctuating selection. Furthermore, target genes, regulated by other genes, were more likely to respond to selection and increase their gene-specific expression noise than regulator genes. These findings show that not just the mean, but also the variance of gene expression level, respond to selection in changing environments, and do so in a network-dependent manner. They further point to gene expression noise as a mechanism for populations to escape extinction by creating phenotypic heterogeneity when faced with environmental changes.

items.title: mFrag: Integrating External DNA Methylation References Improves Lung Cancer Early Detection by Fragmentomics
items.summary: Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag…

research.abstract: Abstract Fragmentomics analyzes features of circulating cell-free DNA fragments (e.g., fragment length or end motifs) derived from whole-genome sequencing of liquid biopsy samples (blood or other body fluids), enabling non-invasive early cancer detection. Here we present mFrag, a framework that integrates external methylation reference atlases with fragmentomic features for lung cancer detection. mFrag comprises two complementary methods: mFrag-Weight, which uses DNA methylation information to weight fragmentomic features, and mFrag-Net, which integrates fragmentomic features and external DNA methylation data through neural networks. We average the output probabilities of the two methods to obtain a final prediction score. The mFrag model was trained using 287 individuals at risk for lung cancer. In an independent case-control testing set comprising 385 non-cancer controls and 46 cancers (28 stage I, 12 stage II, and 6 stage III or IV), mFrag outperforms a DELFI-style fragmentomic approach, improving PR-AUC from 0.455 to 0.720 and sensitivity at 99% specificity from 0.043 to 0.478, with ROC-AUC from 0.871 to 0.908. For stage I lung cancer, mFrag raises PR-AUC from 0.314 to 0.558 and ROC-AUC from 0.855 to 0.894. Applied to end 4-mer motif features, mFrag likewise improved over an unweighted baseline, with gains contributed by both mFrag-Weight and mFrag-Net. In summary, mFrag improves the accuracy of fragmentomics-based lung cancer detection through integrating external DNA methylation data and the complementarity of its two component models, without incurring any additional data-generating cost.

items.title: Extracting and Updating Compact Colored k-mer Indexes
items.summary: Colored k-mer indexes record, for every k-mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new…

research.abstract: Abstract Colored k -mer indexes record, for every k -mer of a collection of genomes, the genomes or species that contain it, and underpin pseudoalignment and sequence search against large collections. Construction of such an index is expensive, yet the collection it represents is rarely final: genomes are retracted or found to be contaminated, users need an index of a single species or clade, and new genomes keep arriving. Rebuilding the index after every such change requires the original sequences and repeats the costly construction. We show that colored indexes based on the spectral Burrows-Wheeler transform (SBWT) can instead be updated efficiently in batches, without the original sequences, and with a result equivalent to the index built from scratch. Given an SBWT and any subset of its k -mers, we first extract the SBWT of this subset directly from the input, in one linear pass and without building a new index. Removing genomes, intersection and difference all reduce to this operation. We then carry the colors through every operation, by finding from the inputs alone where the color sets of the result change, so that removing or extracting genomes, as well as the union, intersection and difference of two colored indexes, each directly yield a complete colored index. In our experiments, editing paid off for large results: removing a genome from an index of 3 682 E. coli genomes took 54 seconds instead of 13 minutes for a rebuild, and adding one took about a minute. On AllTheBacteria, with 192 billion k -mers and 12 733 species, extracting M. tuberculosis , with 180 094 genomes, took less than four hours, and set operations then traced contamination of its color, some of which the next release of AllTheBacteria still contains. Our work turns large colored k -mer indexes from static snapshots of a collection into resources that can be maintained as the collection evolves. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/LoreDepuydt/colored-sbwt-setops .

research.abstract: Background. The American Heart Association defined Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome in 2023. Census-tract studies often examined one condition without spatial modeling. It is unclear where combined Stage 1-2 burden concentrates and how it relates to aging, environment, and socioeconomic conditions. Methods. We built a CKM burden index for 70,336 tracts from five CDC PLACES crude prevalences (obesity, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, chronic kidney disease) and compared it with NHANES 2017-2020. In 69,530 contiguous-U.S. tracts, we fit Bayesian spatial (BYM2) models with demographic, socioeconomic, and environmental predictors and aging x environment interactions, plus descriptive machine learning. The primary model excluded behavioral measures sharing the outcome's BRFSS source; a second added them. Credible intervals (CrIs) are conditional on PLACES estimates. Results. Agreement with NHANES was modest. Burden clustered spatially (Moran's I = 0.657) and highest in the South. Behavioral measures had the largest machine-learning importance (52.6%), partly from shared sourcing. Each percentage-point increase in adults 65 years was associated with 0.112 units higher burden (95% CrI 0.111-0.113) outside low-income, low-access (LILA) tracts. LILA tracts had 0.10-0.14 units higher burden from the 25th aging percentile but not consistently in the youngest decile. Aging and socioeconomic associations held across sensitivity analyses. The primary model's residual Southern excess approached zero after adding behavioral measures, which may reflect shared measurement, real differences in these behaviors, or both. Conclusions. CKM burden is spatially clustered and highest in the South. LILA tracts had modestly higher burden above the youngest tracts. These cross-sectional estimates support area-level surveillance and needs assessment.

However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD). Methods: We tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across…

research.abstract: Background: The gut microbiome is an emerging risk factor for cardiovascular disease. However, there is a lack of large-scale metagenomic studies with replication that identify gut microbial features associated with incident cardiovascular disease (CVD). Methods: We tested for gut microbiome associations with CVD using metagenomes from stool samples in a discovery-replication framework across four large prospective Nordic cohorts with 635 incident CVD in 11,604 participants in the discovery cohort and 2,309 incident CVD in 20,965 participants combined across three replication cohorts. Results: Higher Shannon diversity index and species richness were consistently associated with a lower risk of incident CVD. In addition, the relative abundance of nine species and eleven bacterial functional modules showed reproducible associations with incident CVD in the discovery cohort and in a meta-analysis of the three replication cohorts. We identified a female-specific gut microbiota-related pathway involving the prevalent oral-gut species Rothia mucilaginosa_A, enriched among denture users, thus serving as a proxy for longstanding poor oral health. Mendelian randomization analysis supported a causal effect of denture use on increased relative abundance of Rothia mucilaginosa_A. This pathway was linked to increased CVD risk through altered gut microbial manganese transport, elevated circulating imidazole propionate levels, and increased levels of systemic inflammation biomarkers. The second pathway involved both ?-diversity metrics and the remaining eight species, all of which were strongly associated with multiple markers of metabolic syndrome and with bacterial pathways related to purine metabolism, microbial stress responses, altered redox balance, ascorbic acid degradation, and branched chain amino acid biosynthesis. Conclusions: These findings demonstrate that gut microbiota diversity, specific taxa, and functional pathways provide new insights into the underlying biology of CVD. Furthermore, these findings suggest that the link between poor oral health and cardiovascular disease may, at least partly, operate through altered gut microbiota.

research.abstract: Background: Variation in the gut microbiome composition has been associated with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) in case-control designs. We aimed to investigate associations with incident ASCVD events applying a prospective design to reduce the impact of reverse causality. Methods: We assessed associations between gut microbiome features measured by shotgun metagenomic sequencing and incident total ASCVD, ischemic heart disease (IHD) and ischemic stroke, including fatal and non-fatal events as defined by registry follow-up in 17,216 participants from three Swedish population-based cohorts (SCAPIS, SIMPLER, and MOS). Results from Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for demographic, and lifestyle factors, medication, and prevalent diabetes were combined across cohorts using a fixed-effect meta-analysis accounting for multiple testing. Associations were tested for replication in HUNT and FINRISK. Results: During a median of 6-8 y follow-up, 769 incident ASCVD events occurred. Species diversity was inversely associated with ASCVD and IHD, with a hazard ratio for IHD of 0.86 per SD increase in species richness (95% CI: 0.79-0.95). Sixty-eight common species (i.e., present in ?30% individuals) were associated with incident IHD after adjusting for sex and birth country, but only eight remained in fully adjusted models, including Ruminococcus_B gnavus. Among others, inverse associations were observed for SFEL01 sp004557245 and Fimadaptatus sp900553645 from Christensenellales, an order in which butyrate production has been reported. Streptococcus mutans and Limosilactobacillus fermentum, oral-associated species previously associated with coronary atherosclerosis, were associated with a higher risk of incident IHD, which remained after adjustment for dental health. Replication analysis in the HUNT study supported the finding for S. mutans. No associations were observed with ischemic stroke. Conclusions: Gut species diversity and specific species abundance were associated with incident IHD, providing evidence supporting a protective role of two Christensenellales species and an adverse role of oral species and R. gnavus in the development of IHD.

research.abstract: Background Oropouche virus (OROV) causes recurrent outbreaks in South America, including Colombia. Although Culicoides paraensis is the principal recognized urban vector, the potential involvement of other Culicoides species remains incompletely understood. In Colombia, studies combining viral detection, host-feeding behavior, and ecological suitability are scarce. Methodology We investigated Culicoides communities in urban and peri-urban environments of Puerto Carreno, Vichada, during two seasonal transitions. Species identification combined morphology and COI DNA barcoding, and blood-meal sources were identified using vertebrate molecular markers. OROV RNA was assessed by RT-qPCR targeting the L and S genomic segments, and maximum likelihood prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals were calculated accounting for unequal pool sizes, including a conservative estimate based on concordant detection of both targets. Selected positive samples underwent multiplex amplicon sequencing of fragments from all three OROV genomic segments (L, M, and S) using Oxford Nanopore Technology, followed by consensus reconstruction and phylogenetic analysis. Ecological suitability models were compared with reported OROV case distributions. Principal Findings We collected 1,639 specimens representing 11 taxa, eight supported by COI barcoding. C. insignis accounted for more than 70% of captures and was the only taxon collected in urban settings. OROV RNA was detected in C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi. In C. insignis, concordant detection of the L and S molecular targets yielded an estimated prevalence of 3.61 per 1,000 individuals (95% CI: 0.94-9.60). Nanopore sequencing recovered OROV-derived fragments spanning up to 656 nt across the L, M, and S genomic segments. Shorter fragments supported molecular identification, while phylogenetic analysis of a 656-nt M-segment region recovered from C. insignis and C. pusillus placed both sequences within a group containing viruses associated with the recent South American outbreak, although partial genomic coverage precluded formal lineage assignment. Blood-meal analyses identified feeding on humans, horses, and pigs in C. insignis; humans and horses in C. pusillus; and horses in C. ignacioi. Ecological models identified distinct environmental associations among species, and predicted suitability for overlapping portions of regions reporting OROV cases. Administrative-scale concordance was heterogeneous. Conclusions The integration of molecular, host-feeding, and ecological evidence highlights C. insignis, C. pusillus, and C. ignacioi as species of epidemiological interest in the context of OROV circulation in Colombia. These findings expand current knowledge of OROV-associated Culicoides diversity and provide a basis for targeted entomological surveillance and experimental studies to clarify their potential roles in virus transmission.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Current projections of the prevalence and number of persons with type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) are lacking for Germany. This study aims to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. Methods We used a partial differential equation (PDE) based on the illness-death model to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. The PDE describes the relationship between prevalence, incidence, all-cause mortality and the mortality rate ratio (MRR) of individuals with vs. without type2 diabetes considering age, calendar year and SEP. SEP was measured by quintiles of the German Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation (GISD). Baseline prevalence, incidence, and MRR in 2022 were derived from statutory health insurance data (∼85% of the German population). Projected prevalence was multiplied by population projections from the German Federal Statistical Office to estimate the number of persons with diabetes. Results Type 2 diabetes prevalence increases with age, peaking between 80 and 90 years. Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific prevalence is projected to increase for both sexes across all SEP groups. SEP-related disparities persisted with largest differences between the highest (5th GISD quintile) and lowest (1st GISD quintile) SEP group. The number of persons with type 2 diabetes is projected to rise from 8.4 million in 2022 to between 11.2 and 19.2 million in 2060. Conclusions Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence is projected to increase with increasing socioeconomic inequalities.

research.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 (CYP) genes form a large and functionally diverse superfamily of heme-thiolate monooxygenases that catalyse the oxidation of endogenous and exogenous compounds. Within this superfamily, CYP4 enzymes primarily act on fatty acids, substrates central to energy metabolism. Sustained flight and long distance migration in birds rely on efficient fatty acid use, making CYP4 a pertinent system for examining how lipid associated functions may vary across avian lineages. Here, we characterised the evolution of CYP4 genes across 363 avian whole genomes, representing over 90% of bird families, to investigate patterns of molecular evolution and their association with ecological and life history variation. We identified four CYP4 subfamilies and analysed sequence evolution using site-models, branch-models, and branch-site models. Our analyses revealed conserved elements of the avian CYP4 repertoire alongside lineage-specific heterogeneity in selective constraint. Several amino acid sites under positive selection were located within substrate recognition sites, regions influencing substrate binding and catalysis. Branch-model analyses identified trait-associated variation in selective pressure across feeding habits, migration and primary lifestyle, with gene-specific patterns. Migration-associated differences in ω remained below one, indicating variation in the strength of selective constraint among migration categories. Branch-site analyses revealed evidence of episodic positive selection associated with migratory lineages. Overall, these results highlight site-specific adaptive evolution within CYP4 genes alongside broader variation in selective constraint, providing insight into the evolution of lipid associated metabolic pathways during avian diversification.

research.abstract: Bacterial flagella are rotary nanomachines that enable motility in diverse environments. Although more than 40 genes are required for a functional flagellum in model organisms, only 24 have previously been inferred to be ancestral. Did the last bacterial common ancestor (LBCA) encode a simpler flagellum that was subsequently elaborated, or has its complexity been underestimated because highly diverged homologs are difficult to detect? Here, we combine homology searches across 80,789 bacterial proteomes with conserved sequence signatures, gene-tree clustering, and gene-neighborhood evidence to reconstruct the ancestral flagellum. We identify 49 flagellar protein groups with high-confidence support for ancestral presence across three phylogenetic reconstructions and one additional likely ancestral component, yielding a reconstructed repertoire of 50 ancestral protein groups. This repertoire includes the major structural, export, motor, and assembly components required for a functional flagellum. We provide an interactive database (https://www.flagelladb.org) for exploring the distribution, co-presence, and phylogenetic relationships of flagellar components across bacteria. Our findings indicate that the LBCA possessed a complex, functionally complete flagellar system, substantially exceeding previous estimates of ancestral complexity. The distribution of these components among extant bacteria is consistent with extensive lineage-specific loss and remodeling during subsequent flagellar evolution.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Thyroid dysfunction is a common endocrine comorbidity in type 1 diabetes (T1D), yet most evidence on its burden and biochemical patterns comes from higher-income settings. Data among African children and young adults with T1D remain limited. Objective To determine the prevalence and pattern of thyroid dysfunction and examine demographic and diabetes-related factors associated with thyroid dysfunction among children and young adults with T1D in Kenya. Methods We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among children and young adults with T1D aged ≤34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4) were measured. Thyroid status was classified as euthyroidism (normal TSH and FT4), subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal FT4), overt hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with low FT4), subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH with normal FT4), overt hyperthyroidism (low TSH with elevated FT4), or discordant TSH–FT4 profiles that did not meet these predefined biochemical categories. Prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and multivariable logistic regression examined associations with age, sex and duration of diabetes. Results Among 244 participants with paired TSH and FT4 measurements, 77.5% (n=189) were euthyroid. Twenty-seven participants (11.1%; 95% CI 7.7–15.6%) had biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction: 18 (7.4%) had subclinical hypothyroidism, 5 (2.0%) overt hypothyroidism, and 4 (1.6%) subclinical hyperthyroidism. No overt hyperthyroidism was identified. An additional 28 participants (11.5%) had discordant TSH–FT4 profiles. Hypothyroidism accounted for 85.2% of biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction and was predominantly subclinical (78.3%). Age, sex and duration of diabetes were not significantly associated with thyroid dysfunction in adjusted analyses. Conclusion Thyroid dysfunction affected approximately one in nine Kenyan children and young adults with T1D and was predominantly hypothyroid, particularly subclinical hypothyroidism. Discordant TSH–FT4 profiles were also frequent, underscoring the importance of careful biochemical classification and confirmation of abnormal thyroid-function tests.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes mellitus (DM) is an escalating global public health concern, contributing significantly to global mortalities and posing a major financial burden, particularly in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) like Ghana [Letsa, 2023]. Suboptimal quality of care can lead to severe microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy (DN) and opportunistic infections like urinary tract infections (UTIs) [Letsa, 2023]. DN affects 30–40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, with a reported prevalence of kidney diseases of 12.5% in Ghana [Adoba et al., 2025]. Given that monitoring quality of care is crucial for prevention, this study aimed to evaluate the quality of DM care indicators, particularly focusing on urinary biomarkers, at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital. Methodology A cross-sectional design employing a retrospective medical audit was utilized, assessing patient records at the GPHA hospital Diabetes Clinic. The study population comprised 125 participants whose urinalysis data, demographics, and comorbidity categorization (Diabetes only, Diabetes and Hypertension, Diabetes and Cyesis, etc.) were collected. Urine parameters, including albuminuria, glucose, and Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC), were retrieved from Sysmex’s urinalysis analyzers (Sysmex UC 400, UF 350). Results The study cohort consisted predominantly of females (58.4%, n=73) with a mean age of 54.92 years. The primary diabetic categorization was “diabetes only” (76.8%, n=96). Evaluation of albuminuria showed that mild albuminuria was recorded for only 10.4% (n=13) of participants, and overt albuminuria was absent (0.0%). This mild albuminuria prevalence is notably below the 25–30% global prevalence reported for type 2 diabetics. A significant correlation was established between the various diabetes population categories and urine glucose (Pr=0.001). Pathological RTEC results (> 2.5) were identified in three individuals, primarily from the diabetes and hypertension category (2 individuals) and the diabetes and cyesis category (1 individual). The study noted limitations, including the difficulty in acquiring the specific type of diabetes and the non-availability of data on medication type or complication level. Conclusion The prevalence of mild albuminuria among the study population at the GPHA hospital was significantly lower than established global and certain regional Ghanaian rates. However, the detection of a significant association between diabetic categorization and glucosuria underscores the need for continuous and rigorous monitoring of renal function markers. These findings suggest that while indicators like mild albuminuria may be lower than expected in this specific cohort, targeted interventions remain essential to prevent the progression of renal complications in this high-risk population [ Adoba et al., 2025].

MethodsWe conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed…

research.abstract: Abstract Objective To assess stakeholder acceptability of and preferences for long-acting injectables (LAIs) for tuberculosis (TB) treatment and prevention across World Health Organization regions to inform product development and implementation. Methods We conducted a sequential explanatory mixed-methods study of survey data and qualitative focus group discussions (FGDs). Online surveys assessed perceptions and acceptance of LAIs among two groups: TB programme managers, civil society members and healthcare workers (Survey A), and community members and persons affected by TB (Survey B). Using purposive sampling, survey participants were invited to join FGDs to explore survey findings. Survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics, ordinal logistic regression with stepwise AIC selection, and one-sample proportion tests. FGD transcripts were analysed using modified framework analysis. Findings Among 310 participants (102 Survey A; 208 Survey B), 83% (n=256) favoured LAIs over standard oral TB treatment. Compared with six months of daily oral treatment, 69% preferred a three-month regimen comprising one month of daily oral treatment followed by four injections per monthly visit for two months, while 80% preferred the corresponding regimen with two injections per visit. For prevention, 79% preferred a single injection over one month of oral treatment. In Survey B, interest varied according to lived TB experience, with FGDs suggesting that previous negative experiences with injectables may have contributed to this variation. Conclusion Interest in LAIs for TB treatment and prevention was high, but lower among participants with lived TB experience. Product development and implementation should address concerns about injectables and side effects while preserving patient choice and agency.

research.abstract: Background Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the causative agent of tuberculosis (TB) is able to survive and replicate within host cells of the myeloid cell lineage, a critical step in the development of active TB, achieved through multiple immune evasion mechanisms. TRPML1 (Mucolipin 1), a non-selective Ca 2+ ion channel belonging to the TRP superfamily, is predominantly expressed in innate immune cells and is localized intracellularly along the endosomal–lysosomal continuum. TRPML1-mediated Ca 2+ signalling is vital for lysosomal biogenesis and trafficking processes essential for effective immune responses. The mechanisms regulating TRPML1 channel function in myeloid cells during mycobacterial infection remain poorly characterized. Methods During in vitro infection, TRPML1 expression was modulated in a time-dependent manner by Mtb and M. bovis BCG in murine macrophages, as well as in human neutrophils (PMNs) and macrophages (MDMs). Using pharmacological modulation of TRPML1 channel activity, we observed alterations in intracellular Ca 2+ concentrations following Mtb infection. Results Here, we describe distinct TRPML1 expression patterns in granulomas from TB patients who had completed treatment for active TB, suggesting a potential role for TRPML1 in pathogenesis. We further demonstrate that Mtb infection is associated with altered TRPML1 expression and intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis, accompanied by changes in ROS production, necrotic cell death and enhanced mycobacterial survival within host cells. Treatment of PMN-MDM cocultures with a TRPML1 antagonist, but not an agonist, was associated with increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and necrotic cell death. Discussion Here, we show that Mtb-mediated disruption of TRPML1 function is associated with altered intracellular Ca 2+ homeostasis and may contribute to impaired phagosome maturation, a process previously linked to TRPML1-dependent endolysosomal function, thereby potentially favoring mycobacterial survival within host cells. These findings suggest that Mtb-induced alterations in TRPML1 associated cellular Ca²⁺ homeostasis may impair Ca²⁺-dependent ROS production and cell death, potentially affecting intracellular Mtb survival. Our findings support a role for TRPML1 in maintaining myeloid cell Ca²⁺ homeostasis and suggest that TRPML1 may contribute to the innate immune response to Mtb infection.

research.abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis withstands acidic conditions to survive and replicate within macrophages. To define the genetic determinants of this adaptation, we performed a transposon screen in a lipid-rich, acidic medium that mimics the host environment and supports robust M. tuberculosis growth. This screen identified ldtB , encoding an L,D-transpeptidase, as essential for growth and survival under acid stress. Loss of LdtB decreased 3–3 peptidoglycan cross-linking, disrupted cell wall architecture, and impaired intrabacterial pH homeostasis, resulting in increased susceptibility to cell wall–active antibiotics. Notably, M. tuberculosis lacking LdtB displayed heightened sensitivity to meropenem within macrophages, suggesting that targeting this enzyme could potentiate β-lactam efficacy during infection. These findings establish LdtB as a key mediator linking peptidoglycan homeostasis to acid stress resistance and underscores the importance of in vitro culture models that recapitulate the host microenvironment for uncovering new in vivo active therapeutic targets. Teaser Disabling a key peptidoglycan cross-linking enzyme compromises M. tuberculosis survival under acidic stress and antibiotic exposure.

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin VI, a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin VI and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin VI biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis. Short Summary Integrated genomic and biochemical analyses of Dipsacus asperoides link the predominant accumulation of asperosaponin VI to gene duplication, glycosyltransferase diversification, ordered glycosylation, and root-biased expression. These findings connect genome evolution with specialized metabolic output and identify genes and enzymes useful for engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

research.abstract: Abstract Bacteria can evolve resistance to bacteriophage attack via mutations that alter phage receptors on the cell surface. Flagellotropic phages bind to motility-enabling flagella, creating a potential evolutionary trade-off, since losing flagellar function can reduce fitness in many environments. Phage-resistance studies typically characterize this trade-off using population-mean phenotypes, but selection can act on, and reshape, the underlying single-cell distribution of a trait in ways that mean values alone do not capture. Here, we exploit the well-developed and experimentally tractable model system of Escherichia coli –phage χ (chi) to ask how evolved resistance to a flagellotropic phage reshapes single-cell motility phenotypes, not just their population averages. We experimentally evolved E. coli populations under selection by χ, on soft-agar swim plates which favor motility. Whole genome sequencing revealed early emergence of non-motile mutants with disrupted motility genes, followed by motile, χ-resistant mutants carrying flagellin mutations. Swim-plate assays and single-cell tracking revealed heterogeneous motility outcomes among resistant lineages: some recovered or exceeded ancestor-level motility while others swam slower than ancestors, demonstrating that trade-offs and trade-ups can both arise from selection by the same phage—an outcome rarely captured in a single phage-resistance study. Single-cell tracking further showed that resistant lineages evolved increased tumble bias and altered swimming speed distributions, revealing shifts in trait heterogeneity invisible to mean-based measures. At the ensemble level, resistant mutants also showed remodeled kinase-response output in the upstream chemotaxis signaling pathway, indicating that resistance reshapes motility behavior both through receptor-level and signaling-level adaptation. Together, these findings demonstrate that evolved phage-resistance reshapes the receptor-linked (motility) phenotype across multiple phenotypic scales: from single-cell behavioral distributions to signaling network output, producing diverse and previously undocumented evolutionary outcomes under combined selection pressures. Author Summary Bacteria often rely on flagella, tail-like appendages that enable swimming, to move toward nutrients and escape undesirable environments. Many viruses that infect and kill bacteria (lytic bacteriophages) exploit these motility-enabling flagella to attach to bacterial cells, creating an evolutionary dilemma: a bacterium can become resistant by losing its flagella, but this sacrifices its ability to move. We used experimental evolution to study how motile bacteria respond to attack by such phages. By exposing E. coli to the flagellum-targeting phage χ over many generations, we found that resistance evolved in two stages. Bacteria first became resistant by losing motility entirely, but soon after, motile χ-resistant variants emerged carrying mutations in flagellin, the flagellum’s main building block. Some of these motile-resistant lineages swam even better than their ancestor, while others swam worse, revealing diverse evolutionary solutions to the same selective pressure. Using fluorescence-based signaling measurements, we found that resistant bacteria also altered the internal chemical signaling that controls swimming behavior, not just the physical structure targeted by the phage. These findings reveal how pathogens can retain or even enhance mobility while evading phage attack, with implications for designing phage-based therapies to treat infections by motile pathogens.

items.summary: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its…

research.abstract: Dietary ethanol has long been proposed as a selective force shaping the diets and physiology of tropical frugivores and nectarivores, yet this idea has rested on measurements from only a few species and sites. Here, we present the first global survey of ethanol in wild fruits and flowers (591 and 37 species, respectively, across 18 countries) and test ecological and phylogenetic predictors of its variation. We detected ethanol in the ripened fruits of 72% of angiosperm species (211 species, N [≥] 3 per species; 0.021% - 3.9% alcohol by volume (ABV)). Ethanol was also detected in the flowers of 12 species (0.037% - 0.73% ABV). Maximum fruit ethanol varied with temperature, humidity, and phylogenetic relatedness, and it was higher in ripe fruits collected from the forest floor relative to their canopy counterparts. We then extrapolated potential daily ethanol consumption for 10 primate species. Estimated maximum daily ethanol ingestion for primates ranged from negligible to 0.72 g/kg/day on average (equivalent to 5.1 international standard drinks, 10 g ethanol each, for a 70 kg human). Our findings show that ethanol is widespread in plant reproductive tissues and shaped by both phylogeny and environment, supporting the hypothesis that dietary ethanol has been a pervasive selective pressure on fruit- and nectar-feeding animals.

research.abstract: Abstract Ancestral sequences and substitution histories are usually averaged out in phylogenetic inference and are therefore not reported to the user. However, they can be recovered through ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR) and stochastic character mapping. By implementing and validating a new ASR and stochastic mapping package compatible with both single-locus and multispecies coalescent analysis, we show how reconstructing substitution histories can enhance the information gained about the tempo and mode of molecular evolution. We observe that known substitution histories (simulated and empirical) are recovered more accurately and precisely on time trees compared with unconstrained and non-ultrametric substitution trees that lack temporal directionality (maximum likelihood and Bayesian). We show that codon-partition models with site-rate heterogeneity, based on the four nucleotide characters, can effectively approximate the histories of synonymous and non-synonymous change, while requiring far less runtime than computationally demanding codon models that require 61 characters. In turn, this provides low-bias estimation of dN/dS that is robust to non-stationarity in GC content, codon usage bias, and nucleotide exchangeability rates. Lastly, using three case studies, we demonstrate how the approach can recover expected patterns in molecular evolution and pathogen transmission: that i) smaller-bodied mammalian species tend to have faster synonymous substitution rates than larger relatives, ii) amino acid substitutions are correlated with 3Di structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and iii) influenza A virus spread more frequently to nearby locations than distant ones, in a major H3N2 outbreak in New Zealand. These three trends were more pronounced when based on count estimates derived from stochastic mapping, relative to parametric rates and distances. Our open-source code comes with a user-friendly graphical interface, as the BeastMap package for BEAST 2; supporting a wide range of clock, site, and tree models and data types – including insertions and deletions – within a Bayesian phylogenetic framework.

research.abstract: Abstract Background The plasma proteome may help connect inherited breast cancer susceptibility to biologically interpretable and potentially actionable pathways, but proteome-wide evidence across ancestries remains limited. Methods We conducted proteome-wide Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses of breast cancer risk using cis -protein quantitative trait loci for 1,962 distinct plasma proteins from 34,557 European-ancestry participants in the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project. Breast cancer genome-wide association studies included 156,901 cases and 204,634 controls of European, East Asian, and African ancestries. Ancestry-specific MR estimates were combined by fixed-effects meta-analysis. Candidate proteins were further evaluated through subtype-specific and reverse-direction MR analyses, statistical colocalization, replication in independent European and East Asian proteomic datasets, and analyses of associations between protein polygenic scores and breast cancer status in All of Us. Results Twelve proteins achieved Bonferroni significance in the cross-ancestry meta-analysis ( P < 0.05/1,971 tests), including eight previously reported proteins and four newly prioritized by MR. DNPH1 showed cross-ancestry heterogeneity, while CASP8, RALB, and USP28 showed cross-subtype heterogeneity after accounting for shared controls (all P < 0.05/12). Complementary support varied: six candidates showed strong colocalization (PPH4 ≥ 0.80); four replicated with a consistent direction and nominal significance in deCODE, two in the Japan COVID-19 Task Force, and four in All of Us (all P < 0.05). The strongest cumulative support was observed for LRRC25, PARK7, and LRRC37A2. Conclusions These findings prioritize circulating protein candidates for mechanistic, prevention-oriented, and translational follow-up in breast cancer, while underscoring the need for larger ancestrally diverse proteomic resources to support equitable target and biomarker discovery.

Here, we tracked the longitudinal evolution of three single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses (Drosophila A virus [DAV], Drosophila C virus [DCV], and Nora virus) and one double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus (Bloomfield virus) during persistent…

research.abstract: Abstract Persistent viral infections provide an extended window for viral evolution, yet their intra-host trajectories across the host lifespan remain underexplored. Here, we tracked the longitudinal evolution of three single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) viruses (Drosophila A virus [DAV], Drosophila C virus [DCV], and Nora virus) and one double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus (Bloomfield virus) during persistent infection in Drosophila melanogaster . By analyzing viral populations across early, intermediate, and late infection stages, we mapped dynamic shifts in the viral quasispecies and the emergence of adaptive mutations. These data demonstrate that long-term persistence drives viral evolution in a viral species-specific manner. DAV evolution was defined by clonal interference, driven by the continuous turnover of competing haplotypes. Nora virus exhibited prolonged evolutionary stasis punctuated by a late-stage sweep, suggesting adaptation to the senescing host environment. In contrast, standard DCV populations were locked under strong purifying selection, where no adaptive mutations were detected. However, this constraint collapsed in high-titer DCV infections, triggering extensive mutational diversification. Distinct from the ssRNA dynamics, the multi-segmented dsRNA Bloomfield virus maintained higher sequence fidelity and a stable genomic formula. Ultimately, these results demonstrate that viral evolution during persistent infection is governed by the interplay between specific host-pathogen interactions and the physiological decline of the host.

research.abstract: Empyema necessitans is a rare complication of pleural infection in which infected pleural fluid extends through the parietal pleura into the surrounding soft tissues. We report the case of a 32-year-old man of Indian origin living in the United Kingdom who presented with worsening right-sided pleuritic chest pain, several months of night sweats, and a persistent dry cough. Five months earlier, he had been treated for right-sided pneumonia complicated by a pleural effusion, with persistent radiographic abnormalities on follow-up. Examination revealed reduced right-sided air entry and a tender, fluctuant swelling over the right posterior chest wall. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated a posterior pleural collection extending through the chest wall into the adjacent paraspinal musculature, consistent with empyema necessitans. Ultrasound-guided aspiration yielded frank purulent fluid. Routine bacterial, anaerobic, and fungal cultures were negative. Acid-fast bacilli were not seen on initial microscopy; however, mycobacterial culture became positive after seven days, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing of the pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex. Whole-genome sequencing subsequently identified a lineage 1 East-African-Indian-Ocean isolate with predicted susceptibility to first-line antituberculous agents. Four-drug antituberculous therapy was commenced, with subsequent clinical and radiological improvement. This case highlights chest wall swelling as an unusual presentation of tuberculosis and emphasizes the importance of cross-sectional imaging and targeted mycobacterial testing in establishing the diagnosis.
